News.title: Cruise ship worker, 38, admits having sex with underage girl in his cabin twice as he’s arrested on return to port
News.content:
CRUISE CREEP Cruise ship worker, 38, admits having sex with underage girl in his cabin twice as he’s arrested on return to port

A CREEPY cruise ship lifeguard has admitted to having sex twice with an underage girl in his cabin, police said.

Guatemalan lifeguard Rafael Cayetano Blanco, 38, was cuffed as the MSC World America liner docked at port in Miami.

The accused pervert is now being held on an immigration detainer.



Blanco told cops that he exchanged numbers with a 17-year-old passenger on August 16 – the first day of the cruise.



He admitted that the pair then returned to his cabin to have sex, according to a police report.

She returned to his cabin again three days later and they had sex once again, cops said.

After confessing to both incidents, Blanco was charged with unlawful sexual activity with a minor.



The 38-year-old remains locked up on an immigration hold.

The mega cruise ship can carry more than 6,700 passengers and 2,100 crew.

It set sail from Miami on August 15 before making scheduled stops in Honduras, Mexico and the Bahamas, according to Cruisemapper.

MSC said in a statement: “On discovery of a breach of conduct by a crew member and an alleged criminal act, we immediately contacted the relevant law enforcement authorities.



“We fully supported the investigation and provided every assistance to the guest.

“The crew member concerned has been dismissed.”

It comes after a 25-year-old creep allegedly tried to take pictures up a 13-year-old girl’s dress on a a Royal Caribbean liner.

Matthew Stilwell, 25, from Illinois is accused of trying to take the pervy pictures in a gift shop on the ship.

The teenage girl noticed Stilwell “standing unusually close behind her with the camera application on his cellphone”, according to a police report seen by WPLG.



She told cops he tried to snap a picture at least three times before she ran over to her mum.

Authorities boarded the ‘Allure of the Seas’ when it returned to Port Everglades in Florida, and checked CCTV.

Cops said they found security footage corroborating the young girl’s version of events.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Stilwell allegedly confessed to investigators, but his admission was redacted in the report.

He has since been charged with voyeurism and is currently being held at the Paul Rein Detention Facility in Pompano Beach.

News.title: How Harry’s return can spark dramatic redemption. Hear me out – but the Royal Family NEED pariah prince back in fold
News.content:
SO, the wanderers return. Yes, Harry and Meghan are blighty-bound after the Californian dream imploded and their situation turned as sticky as one of the Duchess’s unsold jams.

Surprise, surprise as soon the pairs drip feed of Royal disses dried up so too did America’s interest – dumped by Netflix and deserted by many of their A-list cronies.





But if America is bored, the UK is rightly aggrieved over the couple’s Megxit U-turn especially when it comes to hapless Harry.

Unlike Meghan, he and the British public have history. In short we once cared which is why his recent betrayals have felt so personal.

Airing the family secrets to the highest bidder during the ailing Queen’s final years squandered his popularity and will be hard to forgive.

Yet, despite this, the stage could still be set for his redemption.

Hear me out. Harry has many flaws but also some key attributes. He has charisma and a natural connection with the public reminiscent of his late mother Diana, a common touch amid the polish and privilege.

Having grown out of the more rebellious excesses of his youth he retains the boyish charm that made him a crowd favourite.

It’s this endearing side that established the goodwill towards him for so long and can still be clawed back if he chooses a more productive return to public life.

And this would be long overdue.





You see, it’s ironic that the title of the duke’s infamous tell-all memoir – Spare – (available in every good charity shop) could in fact have been more accurately applied to his life in LA.

Treading water for six years as Meghan’s plus-one, the fifth in line to the throne so often seemed reduced to a spare part on the sidelines of many tacky stunts and projects.

Remember the 40-year-old’s awkward expression as his wife blabbed to Netflix about her first meeting with late Queen Elizabeth in the 2022 docu-series, Harry & Meghan and reenacted a mocking theatrical curtsy?

Not to mention his toe- curling cameos in her Netflix lifestyle series, With Love.

Ostensibly it was to applaud her brunch-making skills but as always, he seemed he was simply on hand to ramp up the royal connection.

Throughout the sorry mess of Megxit, only Harry’s work with the Invictus Games felt like a rare injection of purpose and positivity – a reminder of where his talents lie and why he can’t be written off yet.

Winning back the hearts of the British people won’t be easy.

The first step will be unlocking his arm from Meghan’s tight grip and forging a more independent path that plays to his strengths.



A greater focus on charity work and building on Diana’s legacy through his support of landmine clearance charity The Halo Trust is an obvious starting point.

Meanwhile, the rumour mill suggests Meghan will find plenty to fill her days, whether that’s a return to the small screen or establishing her own court among other celebrity American expats in the Cotswolds.

No doubt it will involve too many meet-and-greets – the mainstay duty of royal life. From the outset the former Suits star always seemed to be cos-playing at the gig keen to be a Diana 2.0 but with an eye more on the commercial than compassion.

Harry at least appears more authentic and for all the rows and recriminations his absence has been felt.

In the wake of the scandal surrounding Andrew Mountbatten Windsor’s links with convicted paedophile Jeffery Epstein, the Royal family has taken a heavy reputational knock.

Yes, a hardworking King and Queen and a stoic and dedicated William and Kate have successfully steadied the ship but at times it still feels depleted offering.

The line-up would benefit from the different dimension that Harry – ideally freed up from his all consuming legal battles with the press and some of the tedious self-pity – can still offer.

The big question remains just what form this could take.

News.title: I stared Constance Marten in the eyes during horror baby death trial…she’s not evil but this is why she’s STILL a danger
News.content:
CONSTANCE Marten is a criminal I think about often and won’t forget any time soon.

The aristocrat dumped her dead baby daughter in a Lidl Bag for Life while camping in freezing conditions and on the run with convicted rapist husband Mark Gordon.



It was a callous, contemptible and avoidable end to little Victoria’s days-long life.

And, now, Marten, jailed last year for gross negligence manslaughter, wants to appeal her 14-year prison sentence.

I sat through both of her trials at the Old Bailey, which descended into farce, and I am clear she must stay behind bars.



Not because she is a monstrous, evil, wicked mother.

This won’t win me many fans, and maybe I am too woke, but having watched this impulsive, paranoid and wild woman in court for the cumulative best part of a year, I don’t think she is evil at all.

That is too easy and lazy a trope to fall on.

I have sat through horrific, traumatising child murder trials and I have looked evil in the face.

Urfan Sharif, for instance, who tortured his ten-year-old daughter for years before beating her to death, is evil.



Marten is something else.

That ‘something else’ is exactly why she must stay locked up.

She was a selfish, reckless mother.



A failed, absent mother.

A disastrous, barbaric and despicable mother even in how she dumped Victoria’s body.

But not innately evil.

I genuinely believe she at least wanted to be a mother, she wanted to love her children and she believed she could – and that is what makes her so dangerous.

Because the tragedy of this story is that this mentally-troubled woman was fuelled by wild conspiracy theories about Britain’s institutions and a crazy paranoia over her powerful family which blinded her to how terribly and perilously incapable she was of caring for a child.



She prioritised her relationship and genuinely convinced herself she was keeping her kids safe from those who she wrongly thought were ‘out to get’ them – the NHS, social services, the police, the family courts.

It is hard for any normal person like you or I to even try to understand how on earth she thought that – it is one of the craziest things I have seen in court – but she very clearly did.

She thought she was showing her children love and, in doing so, failed to protect her them from herself.

If she gets out soon, I fear history could repeat itself.



After all, having a family was the whole, entirely misguided point of her and husband Mark Gordon’s secret sprint across the country.

They had already had four children taken away by the oh-so-terrible family courts and Marten genuinely thought going on the run was an act of love to get her family away.

It is a delusion that led her daughter to die in a freezing tent but, even through two trials, Marten just could not accept it.

Victoria’s death in 2023 was the most horrific end and there were warning signs years earlier.



In 2017, in labour with her first child, Marten went to a hospital in Wales with a fake name – Isabella O’Brien – and a fake Irish accent, claiming to be a traveller outcast from her family.

It did not take long for NHS staff to recognise her from a nationwide alert that was put out after she disappeared while heavily pregnant.

Social services went to where she was staying and found they had been camping in the woods, with bottles of urine on the floor by the entrance.

A disgraceful way to live ahead of the birth of her first baby, which tragically foreshadows the circumstances in which her last baby will die.

But this way of life wasn’t the act of an evil woman intent on harming her first baby.



She was on the run with warped fears that her wealthy family had hired private investigators to spy on her and Gordon – a convicted rapist whom her family hated.

Family court proceedings began after their first baby, and continued in London when the couple moved there.

Judges note that Gordon could be violent when under stress, and that the couple sometimes prioritised their own relationship over their baby’s needs.

By late 2019, Marten was already pregnant with her second baby.

A local authority alleged domestic abuse between her and Gordon, that they failed to meet their children’s medical needs and that they tried to avoid investigation.



And later a heavily pregnant Marten fell out of a window in the early hours.

Gordon did not call 999.

Their baby survived and they told authorities she fell out the window while trying to fix the TV aerial.

Authorities remained suspicious.

Marten left hospital and fled to Ireland with her two children, before returning a month later when they were taken off her.



By January 2021, their third baby was born and also removed.

They repeatedly missed contact sessions with their children and then stopped visiting altogether before a judge decided in January 2022 that all four children – yes, they had had another by this point – would be permanently removed and adopted.

Throughout the family court proceedings, Marten and Gordon stuck loyally together against social workers, the NHS, the police, the family court system who they thought were not there to help but to destroy them.

They genuinely thought it was them and their family against the world, and this same, selfish, deluded attitude was on show at the Old Bailey.

As family court Judge Reardon said: “The strong impression given by the parents is that of two people who are fiercely united in an unrelenting struggle against a non-existent opponent.”



Marten, so desperate to keep her children, offered to separate from Gordon. Luckily, the Judge did not believe her.

But then we come to Christmas Eve 2022.

Marten and Gordon had spent nine months hiding their fifth pregnancy, knowing that it would be taken away if anyone found out.

They jumped between councils so none could claim authority, and ended up giving birth in a holiday cottage in Northumbria.

Days later on January 5 2023 were driving along the M61 motorway near Bolton in Greater Manchester when their Peugeot 206 went up in flames.



Another driver had pulled over and called 999.

Marten, knowing their baby would be taken away, made the selfish, reckless and dangerous choice to run.

They travelled from Bolton, to Liverpool, to Harwich in Essex, spending hundreds in taxi fares with cash.

They then went to London, before getting a tent and camping in the South Downs in freezing temperatures that would never in a million years be suitable for a newborn.

Victoria would die there.



She would be dumped in a Lidl Bag for Life and would not be found until March 1, in a disused allotment.

She was so decomposed that we cannot know for sure when she was born or when she died.

All we will ever know for sure is her name.

It was obviously never Marten and Gordon’s plan to end up there.

They obviously didn’t have much of plan – she mentioned wanting to sneak abroad – but it certainly was not to end up there.



Long before that car caught fire, but certainly as soon as it did, they should have accepted their time was up and hand their baby over.

Instead, they decided the opposite and selfishly chose to take their baby on the run. Part of this decision-making was no doubt because of those warped delusions that the authorities were the callous ones and she had to protect her family from being broken up again.

So extreme were her delusions that she would rather camp with a newborn in winter than turn themselves in. She thought this was her being a protective mother. How sad.

But even if, when that car caught fire and they saw their plans go up in smoke, they did stop and hand the baby over. What then? Would they try again for a sixth baby and do the same? Or a seven? Or an eighth?

And then she may hide them in that strange way she calls love and we could be in the same situation.



Throughout both their trials it was so clear that they still genuinely think they are the loving parents and that all the institutions were in the wrong.

She even blamed the press for publicising the police’s manhunt, because it apparently made them panic which is why they wanted to lie low on the South Downs.

They failed to show any remorse or take any accountability for how their own reckless actions killed her daughter.

She still, remarkably, was convinced she was showing her child love and was quite angry that others could not see that.

That is why she must stay behind bars.



This is a woman not motivated by evil wickedness, but by a hopeless, dangerous desire to be the sort of mother she thinks she is but will never be.

So much so that she had five children in a relatively short space of time and ran away with one.

She is clearly an awful mother and I can’t imagine much has changed in the year since she was sentenced. I genuinely hope she can come round to seeing what really went wrong. But I just don’t think that will happen anytime soon.

So if she gets out, she may well try for another.

If she does, she may well hide it again from the authorities.



And we may well end up with another avoidable tragedy.

News.title: Can I collect fallen fruit from a neighbour’s overhanging tree? Full rules explained
News.content:
AUGUST marks the peak of harvest season and trees across the nation are beginning to bear fruit.

But while it may be tempting to pick your neighbour’s juicy produce, doing so could land you in serious legal trouble.

In the UK, there are a whole host of laws protecting an individual’s property – and fruit trees are no exception.



Although your neighbour’s tree may overhang into your garden, you are not entitled to the legal right to pick and keep their produce – no matter how far their branches encroach onto your property.



As the fruit remains the property of the tree owner, taking it without explicit permission can be considered theft.

It can even be the subject of civil action in court, amounting to a legal order of financial compensation or returning the stolen property.

This law applies even where the fruit has been severed from the branch.



According to arboricultural consultants, Hellis Solutions, whether the fruit has “fallen from being ripe or been blown off by the wind, or severed by the act of man”, it still belongs to the tree owner.

In these cases, your neighbour has the right to enter your garden to retrieve their fallen fruit.

Alternatively, you are able to collect their produce and offer it back to your neighbour.

The only exception is if the fruit is growing on public land.



Under the Theft Act 1968, picking wild-growing fruit, flowers, foliage, or mushrooms for personal consumption is not considered stealing.

News.title: Harrowing moment dad who left daughter to die in hot car while he watched porn is found dead by horrified nanny
News.content:
‘HE’S NOT BREATHING’ Harrowing moment dad who left daughter to die in hot car while he watched porn is found dead by horrified nanny

A NEWLY surfaced 911 call has revealed the moment a dad who left his daughter to die in a hot car while he watched porn is found dead by their nanny.

Christopher Scholtes, 38, took his own life in the garage of his £750,000 Arizona home in 2025 – a year after two-year-old Parker’s death.



The little girl died in the back of the family vehicle when Scholtes left her alone on the afternoon of July 9, 2024, as temperatures soared to 42C.

Scholtes took his own life by gassing himself with a car exhaust pipe the day he was set to attend his sentencing.



He faced up to 30 years behind bars.

Chilling never-before-heard audio captured the moment the nanny found his lifeless body.



She is heard saying: “He’s in our home garage. It’s suicide, it’s suicide.

“He’s not breathing, and I can’t find a pulse.”



The carer is then heard telling cops that smoke is coming out of the garage and into the property.

She continues in a panic: “I got them up to get the girls out, but they haven’t, like, gotten the girls out – like everything is kind of chaotic.”

The babysitter adds: “It [the garage] was locked and I had to get the keys to open the garage door and then I found him in there.

“He was supposed to… he had to surrender tomorrow.”

Scholtes, who had a habit of leaving his kids in the car, had pleaded guilty to second-degree murder one month earlier.



Authorities argued Scholtes had left Parker inside the family’s Acura in the driveway of their Marana home near Tucson.

He claimed to have left the toddler in the car at around 12:30pm for 30 minutes with the air conditioning on.

Scholtes claimed he did this as he didn’t want to wake her up from a nap.

Court records later revealed the girl had actually been left alone in the vehicle for over three hours.

He later admitted to knowing the car would automatically turn off its air-con within 30 minutes.



After leaving the car, Scholtes went inside his home to watch porn, play video games and drink beer.

Meanwhile, Parker was left roasting to death inside the car and wasn’t rescued until her mum returned home at around 4pm that day.

Bodycam footage from responding officers showed Scholtes plead with cops and claim he’d only left her outside for “no more than 30, 45 minutes”.

Police told Scholtes at the time: “She’s very hot right now. We’re going to do everything we can.”

Another one of his daughters told police: “My dad started screaming cause he walked outside and he saw that she was in the car still, her lips were purple and she wasn’t breathing.”



After she was found in the car, Parker was rushed to hospital but died within an hour.

A suicide note was left inside the home and Scholtes left a living will on top of the car in case he survived the suicide attempt disabled.

His other children from a previous marriage told cops he would often leave them in the car when they were young.

And Parker’s biological siblings also told police their father regularly left all three of them strapped in the car while he left to run errands.

Scholtes’ own texts with his wife revealed some of his habits.



His partner Erika said in one message after Parker’s death: “I told you to stop leaving them in the car.

“How many times have I told you?”

He responds: “Babe, I’m sorry. Babe, our family. How could I do this? I killed our baby, this can’t be real.”

Medical examiner Daniel Casa claimed Scholtes had begun making suicidal remarks following his daughter’s death.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

She also catalogued Scholtes’ long list of health conditions, including depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder and ADHD.

News.title: How former lads’ holiday hotspot became a ‘ghost town’ as strict alcohol bans, cop patrols & £3k fines leave bars empty
News.content:
MUSIC is blaring, strobe lights are glaring and the odd drunken boy is spinning on a street corner – but it’s not quite the notorious strip it once was.

A huge revamp has swept across this once-raucous resort and it now seems the classic British “lads’ holiday” no longer fits the luxury image being carefully cultivated by this former party destination.





The nostalgic drive up to Magaluf, in Majorca, didn’t quite give me the same feeling either. Once, leaving the polished luxury of Palma and heading towards the strip felt like an instant shift into chaos.

Now, that jarring contrast has been softened by gleaming five-star hotels and streets that are, at the very least, noticeably cleaner.

There was no sense that this was the place where 18-year-olds who had just broken free from school would come to let loose, away from their loved ones, for the first time.

I’m walking up the strip and it’s almost midnight. I’ve seen more police cars than I have promoters – the first buzzkill for the thrill-seeking tourists who once descended here in their thousands.

The odd promoter does approach me, but with the enthusiasm of someone going through the motions. The old hard-sell tactics and relentless harassment have all but disappeared because there are barely enough revellers to tempt into the bars.

No drunken teenagers are snapping up two-for-one deals, stumbling through the doors giggling, or clutching their friends’ hands as they weave through crowds of 100s to claim their free shot at the bar.

Instead, I was greeted by families and toddlers who had taken their children to the strip for perhaps a glimpse of the lights and a little wander around the empty chairs scattered along the promenade.

This year, authorities in Spain’s Balearic Islands tightened their grip on an alcohol law first introduced in 2020 in parts of Majorca, including Magaluf.





As well as banning drinking on public roads, the rules prevent shops from selling alcohol late at night while imposing tighter controls on party boats.

Any tourists caught breaking the rules could face a fine of up to €3,000.

Palma mayor Jaime Martínez said one of his main objectives is to “correct uncivil attitudes”.

The new clampdown has clearly deterred some tourists, particularly Brits, who bar workers say are no longer flocking to Magaluf in the numbers they once did.

The town has shifted from a budget party strip into a modernised resort zone called Calvià Beach.

Backed by more than €230million in public and private investment, the multi-phase revamp focuses on upscale hotels, upgraded infrastructure and family-friendly cultural spaces.

Emma, 25, a bartender on the strip, told me: “The lack of tourists is definitely affecting business.

“Magaluf has lost all business and its target audience following the revamp.



“British people don’t come at all anymore, it’s only British families and their children.”

Emma, who has been working on the strip for almost a decade, said she used to see all sorts of British boys causing chaos.

She recalled a time when she and her friends had gone to party at one of the bars and ended up in a physical fight with a group of Brit boys.

She described how the Brits, aged between 25 and 35, began throwing chairs at the girls.

Emma said: “Locals have grown tired of the way the tourists act in Majorca.

“It’s like a tourist dumpster and they behave in ways they wouldn’t in their own country.



“That’s why they have tightened the laws but it also means they don’t want to come anymore because they can’t treat it like a dumpster.”

Simon Hood, Executive director of John Mason International, has also issued a warning to Brits jetting off to the party destinations of Majorca and Ibiza in the coming months.

The travel expert said holidaymakers should avoid public drinking and excessive noise at night if they want to avoid penalties, with authorities planning stronger enforcement of key laws throughout the summer.

I found one Brit sitting, sober, in an empty area of the infamous – but now deserted – Piano Bar, while his friends had decided to head further along the strip in search of a bar where there was actually a crowd.

Ben told me: “I came here thinking it would be more wild than this but it’s dead. It’s midnight, where is everyone?”

When I asked him how he felt about the strict alcohol ban, he said: “I don’t even care about that, but clearly others do, that’s why no one’s here,” before laughing.

He added: “My sister came here back in the day, the way she described it is nothing like this.”

Patrolling the top half of the strip, I managed to grab a couple of police officers who had pulled up in their car and were quietly observing the subdued scenes.

One told me: “We have special police just for this area.”

He said that at night there are around six police officers constantly walking up and down the strip.



“It’s to deter criminals,” he told me.

And the clampdown appears to match the figures, with last year being the town’s best tourist season on record in terms of public order.

The number of offences reported to Calvià Police fell 30 per cent across July and August compared with the previous year.

Tiger Tiger was my next nostalgic destination, once booming with tourists and now reminiscent of a movie scene with tumbleweeds drifting across the screen.

Josh, 26, a promoter standing outside the bar, told me: “It’s dying down and it’s not what it used to be. It’s really expensive here now. I’d say prices are pretty similar to Ibiza.

“The police have cracked down a lot on partygoers, and it’s generally deterred rough people.”



Bartender Amine told me as he shook a cocktail: “This summer has felt more strange than ever.”

The 22-year-old added: “There’s absolutely no British tourists anymore. I think it’s because it’s too expensive now.”

The resort’s reinvention shows little sign of slowing.

More than 60 per cent of its hotels are now four and five-star properties, while Calvià council has calculated that the resort managed to halve the decibel levels produced by Magaluf businesses compared with 2024.

Even the town’s attractions have acquired a more polished sheen.

Black metal stands now punctuate the streets as part of a new “selfie route”, directing visitors towards designated vantage points where they can photograph the beach, the sea and tiny Sa Porassa island, or climb into the hills behind the hotels for a panoramic view.

It’s now 1am and the strip has finally begun to stir.

A few more bodies had drifted into the disco-lit streets, but the atmosphere remained a pale echo of the electric frenzy that once made Magaluf infamous.



Earlier, we had eaten beside the newly renovated seafront – another symbol of a resort attempting to redraw its own identity.

For years, Magaluf was regarded as one of Spain’s most notorious holiday destinations, its name practically shorthand for sunburnt excess, cheap booze and badly behaved British tourists.

Its history, however, explains why the transformation has been so dramatic.

During the tourism boom of the 1960s and 70s, Magaluf rapidly blossomed into a major holiday destination. Hotels multiplied, businesses flourished and tourism became a lucrative economic engine for the local community.

But as the years passed, quantity began to eclipse quality.

What had started as a sun-drenched Mediterranean success story gradually mutated into a party capital whose reputation became inseparable from its excesses.

It was routinely mentioned alongside Benidorm and Lloret de Mar as a byword for unruly mass tourism, while the resort repeatedly made headlines over balconing deaths, brawls and alcohol-fuelled excess.

But that version of Magaluf increasingly feels like a relic.

Today’s Calvià Beach – the new brand name adopted by hotel chain Meliá International – is cleaner, quieter and considerably more manicured, and it seems Brit teens don’t want any part of it.

News.title: Ex-soldier ‘murdered gran, 75, and battered her husband with metal pole after bursting into their home during burglary’
News.content:
OAP TRAGEDY Ex-soldier ‘murdered gran, 75, and battered her husband with metal pole after bursting into their home during burglary’

A FORMER soldier allegedly murdered a great-grandmother and battered her husband with a metal pole during a burglary, a court heard.

Rose Smith, 75, and Ronald Smith, 81, were watching TV in Finsbury Park, North London, when four men burst in and made demands for cash, it is said.

The gran was found collapsed in a hallway at around 9.20pm on August 11 after a neighbour flagged down police.

Rose was rushed to hospital but tragically could not be saved and was declared dead the following day.





A post-mortem examination gave the preliminary cause of death as a stroke, which the prosecution alleges was caused by the incident.

Jeffrey Dean Rose, 46, appeared at Barkingside Magistrates’ Court today charged with manslaughter, assault occasioning actual bodily harm and aggravated burglary with intent.

The court was told a man armed with a metal police attacked Ronald, who “had to raise his arms to protect his face”.

Prosecutor Grace Bussey said: “They were told to sit on the sofa and their phones were taken off them.



“When Mrs Smith left the living room she collapsed in the hallway.”

Suzanne John, defending, said dad-of-two Jeffrey Rose was a private investigator from 2012 to 2016.

She told the court he then became a soldier but was discharged due to the Covid pandemic and instead became a bin man.

The defendant was remanded in custody to appear at the Old Bailey on September 22.



In a statement, Rose’s family said: “This is the most devastating loss our family could ever have imagined.

“Rose was a truly wonderful, outgoing woman who was loved by so many people.

“She loved bingo, going to cafes with her friends and, above all, spending time with her family.

“She treasured the time she spent with her children, grandchildren and great-grandchild.

“She was the life and soul of every party. She had a wonderful personality, a big heart and a way of bringing laughter and happiness wherever she went.



“We want people to remember Rose for the person she truly was — loving, fun, kind, sociable and full of life.”

News.title: Madeleine McCann suspect Christian Brueckner to face retrial over rape in ‘game changer’ for missing toddler case
News.content:
OFFICIALS are set to send Christian Brueckner back to court over rape claims and reignite the Madeleine McCann case against him.

Germany’s top prosecutor has secured a hearing to tell an appeal judge Brueckner, 50, should not have been cleared of rape in 2024 – and must face a retrial.



Crucial evidence with the power to put Brueckner behind bars for good was revealed to have been left out of the trial by The Sun – and could now finally be used against him.

The hearing announcement, set for January, has been hailed by Maddie investigators in Europe as “a game changer” as they realise a retrial will almost certainly follow under the German system.



A second trial is seen as crucial for the McCann case as it could put fiend Brueckner in jail for good. That is when investigators have said they would finally charge the sex offender over Maddie.

A source close to the case in Germany said: “This is a case with very little good news – and no prospect of a happy outcome.



Watch The Sun’s documentary: Madeleine McCann: The Evidence on Prime Suspect Christian Brueckner

“But for those who want to see Brueckner charged over Madeleine, this new court date is a gamechanger.

“The way the German system works means every part of the original trial will be considered – and the judge overseeing it is incredibly sharp. She will miss nothing.

“Maddie investigators realise for the first time, there is a genuine will to see a retrial and for something to be done about Brueckner.”



Drug dealer Brueckner was cleared of the rape of Irish holiday rep Hazel Behan in 2024 allowing him to sensationally be freed last year.

He has now been ordered to appear before a court in Leipzig at the start of next year in front of one of Germany’s leading appeal judges, Judge Loisa Bartel.

A decision on the appeal would follow in as little as a few days. It means Brueckner could face a second rape trial as soon as next spring – although he would not be held on remand.



A letter from the court to expected attendees reads: “Criminal proceedings against Christian Stefan Brueckner for aggravated rape, among other offences.

“In the above-mentioned criminal proceedings, the scheduling of the main hearing of the appeal on points of law (Revision) concerning the appeals lodged by the Public Prosecutor’s Office and the private accessory prosecutors (Nebenklägerinnen) is now pending.

“The main appeal hearing is therefore to take place in front of the Federal Administrative Court in Leipzig on Monday, 11 January 2027.”

Prosecutors in Germany still believe he kidnapped and killed Madeleine, three, in 2007 – while British cops have also stepped up their enquiries into the paedophile and are looking at the possibility of extraditing him to the UK.

Their tactic has been to secure a second rape conviction against the sicko that would allow a court to cage him for life – and embolden German cops to prosecute him over the McCann case.



As long as Brueckner remains free cops remain panicked he could flee Germany and go into hiding – a tactic he has used in the past when facing suspicion over crimes.

Rolling 24-hour police surveillance of Brueckner was scrapped earlier this year raising fears tracking the sex offender could finally slip out of the country.

But this has now been reinstated, however, as German officials realise it is essential for preserving the suspect’s safety in the wake of low-level vigilante attacks.



Brueckner has been laying low since publicly declaring he “f***ing hates Maddie” in a vile video outburst published on YouTube.

Three-year-old Madeleine, of Rothley, Leics., vanished from the Ocean Club, in Praia da Luz, Portugal on May 3 2007 while on holiday with her family.

Brueckner was named as the prime suspect in the disappearance and murder of the tot in 2020 by German cops.

Police have been able to confirm his phone was near Ocean Club, where the McCanns were staying, around the time Madeleine disappeared on May 3, 2007.

Witness Helge Busching claims a year later Brueckner all-but-confessed to him at a music festival, in Spain, saying “she didn’t scream” as the pair discussed the McCann case.



Investigators say they have physical evidence Madeleine is dead but no forensic proof tying Brueckner to the case.

An exclusive Sun investigation – aired as a Channel 4 documentary in May – revealed cops are in possession of images that help contribute to their understanding Maddie is dead.

They also have appalling child abduction stories where Brueckner daydreams about snatching and abusing young girls – including one outside a kindergarten.

He even brags about his desperation to “take something small and use it for days” in online chats with another paedophile.

Despite the overwhelming circumstantial evidence, investigators have been reluctant to chargeover the casess, fearing the lack of forensic evidence would harm their chances.



They were also spooked by a court clearing Brueckner of rape and a string of sex assaults last year – the acquittal which put him on the path to freedom.

Since Brueckner’s release, the Met have significantly stepped up their activity on the case, including jetting to Portugal last year to re-interview witnesses, as revealed by The Sun.

Last week we told how UK cops had taken possession of bombshell files on Brueckner from Germany.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Brueckner has refused to answer police questions over the case but has insisted he is innocent in letters. His lawyers continue to protest his innocence on all matters.

He was released from prison on September 17 when his seven-year sentence for the 2005 rape of a woman, 72, in Praia expired, with German cops insisting their Maddie investigation would continue.

News.title: Father's house rammed before son died in A66 crash
News.content:
A house rammed by a car before the fatal A66 crash in Middlesbrough belonged to the father of a teenager who died in the incident.

Cole Worthy, 17, was one of five young men who died when a Volkswagen Passat travelling in the wrong direction hit a Cleveland Police armed response vehicle, also killing two police officers.

Before the crash at 03:39 BST on Saturday, police had received multiple reports of two cars driving dangerously around the town and a Volvo XC60 was seen ramming properties.

The BBC understands that, after his father's home was rammed, Worthy and the four others set out in the Passat. Police said they were linking the activities of the Volvo XC60 and the Passat.

There is no suggestion Worthy's father was involved in criminal activity.

PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died in the crash, as did Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and Worthy.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct said officers had been pursuing the Passat for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when it turned on to the dual carriageway.

Both vehicles were operating with cloned number plates but were picked up by automated number plate recognition technology.

News.title: Trump says all mines cleared from Strait of Hormuz
News.content:
US President Donald Trump has said that the US Navy has removed or detonated all mines in the Strait of Hormuz - the vital waterway which Iran has largely closed since the beginning of the war in the Middle East.

"Iran has been notified that any ship or boat placing new mines will be immediately and systematically destroyed," Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform.

There is no comment from Iran.

Closure of the strait has caused wild fluctuations in the price of oil on world markets. Trump has often said the US has control of the area - but Iran has fired against vessels it says have sought to cross without its permission.

Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to transit the Strait of Hormuz before the war, which began on 28 February with US and Israeli air strikes against Iran.

In addition to closing the strait, Iran retaliated against Israel and against US bases in the region as well as US Arab allies in the Gulf.

A ceasefire aimed at facilitating talks to end the war has collapsed and there has been intermittent exchange of fire between the US and Iran.

However, this week the US announced a raft of economic sanctions against Iran.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that any nation financially partnering with Iran would be isolated.

Iran and the US signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) in June - a 14-point document which set a 60-day deadline to reach a deal on the Strait of Hormuz, before substantial negotiations on resolving the nuclear issue - allegations that Iran is building a nuclear weapon, which Tehran has consistently denied.

However, that deadline has now expired and talks have collapsed leading to the new US sanctions that Trump believes will lead to the collapse of the Iranian regime.

Iran has been under sanctions for most of the time since the founding of the Islamic Republic in 1979 and Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said Tehran was "fully prepared" for the wider sanctions, which he added would lead to "another defeat" for the US.

Its economy, however, has suffered as a result of the war - and a blockade of Iranian ports that the US has been maintaining for weeks not to allow trade to continue.

On Tuesday, China - the biggest buyer of Iranian oil - said it was firmly opposed to what it called the US's "illegal unilateral sanctions" and would take "all necessary measures" to safeguard its rights.

The US announcement comes ahead of planned talks between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month.

Washington is likely to be wary of potential retaliation from Beijing, which processes the majority of the world's rare earths and other critical minerals, crucial in the manufacture of many high-tech products.

Beijing has already tightened export controls on rare earths as part of previous trade negotiations with the US.

News.title: Who does Iran trade with and what could Trump's 'economic D-Day' mean?
News.content:
The US has said "the single greatest financial offensive ever" will help it and Israel end their ongoing war with Iran.

However, Iran is no stranger to these tactics.

The regime has faced near continuous US sanctions since the Islamic Revolution of 1979. In that time, it has developed deep trade ties with several countries which either have a history of ignoring US economic pressure themselves or cannot afford to stop trading with Iran.

As a result, Iran says it is "fully prepared" for the new US sanctions and many economists argue the impact of Washington's latest move will be limited.

So, who does Iran trade with? And could what the US has called an "economic D-Day" have any real impact on Iran?

News.title: Man dies in crash after police pursuit
News.content:
A man has died and two women have been injured in a crash after a police pursuit near Stratford-upon-Avon.

Officers tried to stop a black Audi on Birmingham Road shortly before 17:30 BST on Monday but the driver failed to pull over, Warwickshire Police said.

A pursuit began and 15 minutes later the Audi crashed into a white Ford Puma, the force added, with the Audi's 19-year-old male driver confirmed dead at the scene by paramedics.

The driver of the Ford, a woman, was seriously injured and remains in hospital in critical condition, while injuries to a second woman - her passenger - were serious but not believed to be life-threatening. An investigation by the police watchdog is under way.

Officers said after failing to stop, the Audi made off in the direction of the A46 before travelling back towards Stratford on the A439 Warwick Road where the crash occurred.

A number of other cars were damaged during the pursuit, police said.

Warwick Road was closed on Monday from the Marraway roundabout to its junction with Ingon Lane and Sand Barn Lane, with the stretch remaining shut on Tuesday morning.

It has since reopened.

News.title: Yellow weather warnings issued as thunderstorms and flooding forecast
News.content:
Yellow weather warnings have been issued by the Met Office as heavy rain and thunderstorms are forecast to break out over parts of the UK later this week.

The warnings span Wednesday and Thursday and include parts of east Wales, the Midlands, northern England, East Anglia and southern England - including London.

It is likely to be the one of the most widespread outbreaks of heavy rain across southern and central parts of the UK this summer.

While good news for regions plagued by drought, significant accumulations could lead to flash flooding where the ground is too dry and hard to absorb the downpours. Lightning, large hail and gusty winds are also possible.

News.title: Young people leaving care have death rate four times higher than national average
News.content:
Young adults who have left care have a death rate around four times higher than the general population, a new review, external shows.

Often left alone "with no safety net," the report says the consequences can be catastrophic.

On turning 18, people leaving care in England often lose "significant levers of support", the Government-commissioned report concluded, as it warned the so-called "care cliff" must be addressed.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4 Today, report co-author and broadcaster Ashley John-Baptiste, who grew up in care, called the deaths a national tragedy.

There were 112 deaths of care leavers aged 18 to 24 notified in 2025, which the review said equalled about 130 deaths per 100,000 care leavers.

John-Baptiste recalled his own experience of turning 18 and moving out of the last of four foster homes he'd lived in.

"I was made to live alone and work out how to be an adult," he said.

Unable to afford a bed frame, he says he slept on a mattress on the floor of his council flat and felt a deep sense of abandonment and isolation.

News.title: US judge rejects Ghislaine Maxwell's 'frivolous' appeal against conviction
News.content:
Ghislaine Maxwell's latest bid to overturn her sex trafficking conviction has been rejected by a US judge, who dismissed her claims as "frivolous" and "meritless".

The 64-year-old is serving a 20-year prison sentence for her role in procuring girls for the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein after being found guilty in December 2021.

Maxwell had appealed against her five felony convictions, claiming her constitutional rights had been "violated in multiple respects".

But a New York judge flatly rejected the appeal, describing it as "lengthy and rambling".

Maxwell said Epstein-related documents released by the US Justice Department earlier this year supported her case that she had been wrongly convicted.

But the judge ruled that "far from exculpating her, it incriminates her or reinforces the correctness" of her conviction.

The judge also said her appeal "falls very far from the mark", adding: "Nearly all its claims are procedurally barred; the overwhelming testimonial and documentary evidence adduced at trial conclusively established her guilt; and her petition's claims are demonstrably meritless, and generally based on speculation, distortions, and/or outright falsehoods.

"There is no fact that Maxwell fairly puts in dispute that has any potential to disturb the outcome of her trial."

The judge warned Maxwell against making further appeals, saying it "would not be taken in good faith" by the court.

Maxwell was found guilty in 2021 of facilitating Epstein's abuse. Prosecutors said she recruited and groomed girls, some as young as 14, between 1994 and 2004, before they were abused by Epstein, who died in prison in 2019.

Maxwell appeared virtually before the US House Oversight Committee in February this year but refused to answer questions, invoking her right to remain silent as she pleaded the Fifth Amendment.

Republican House Oversight Committee chairman James Comer said the situation was "very disappointing", adding: "We had many questions to ask about the crimes she and Epstein committed, as well as questions about potential co-conspirators."

Maxwell has previously sought a pardon from US President Donald Trump.

When asked last October whether he would consider pardoning Maxwell, Trump said he "wouldn't consider it or not consider it", adding: "I don't know anything about it, so I will speak to the [Department of Justice]."

The US Senate last month passed a resolution declaring its opposition to a presidential pardon for Maxwell.

News.title: Inspectors to assess police after Henry Nowak murder
News.content:
An inspection into how a police force responds to violent incidents has been launched in the wake of Henry Nowak's murder.

The 18-year-old student was stabbed in Southampton by Vickrum Digwa, who lied to police and insisted he had been the victim of a racist attack.

Hampshire Police officers initially arrested Nowak and placed him in handcuffs as he lay dying.

His Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Service (HMICFRS) will assess the force's processes, training and how officers are supported to make sound and impartial judgements.

The inspection was requested by Hampshire Police and Crime Commissioner Donna Jones, who said the public "must have confidence" in the force.

"This inspection will provide an independent assessment of the force's training, processes and culture, including the handling of allegations of racially aggravated assault," she said.

"Henry's family deserve answers, and the public deserve reassurance that their police service is equipped to recognise victims and provide the highest standard of care when it matters most."

News.title: Boy, 3, injured in crocodile attack returns home
News.content:
A three-year-old boy who was seriously injured in a crocodile enclosure has been discharged from hospital and is settling back in at home, his family has said.

The child returned home "a few weeks ago" and is "happy to be home, playing with his toys, sleeping in his own bed and being a big brother", his parents said in an update posted online.

The boy was visiting Johnsons of Old Hurst near Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, with his family on 18 June when he was attacked by at least one of the animals.

In an update shared on a fundraising page on Monday, the boy's family said it was "nice to have us all back together in the comfort of our own home".

Cambridgeshire Police arrested and bailed a 30-year-old man from Norfolk on suspicion of attempted murder after the incident.

News.title: Legendary rugby league winger Boston dies aged 92
News.content:
Tributes have been led by prime minister Andy Burnham who said he was a "giant of a man in every way".

"Heartbroken to hear my friend Sir Billy Boston has died," he said on social media.

"Billy was one of the greatest rugby league players of all time but also one of the kindest and most down-to-earth people you could ever wish to meet.

"He always had time for people and gave so much to back to his adopted home, Wigan.

"I will miss him greatly and am thinking today of Billy's family, still grieving the recent loss of his beloved wife Joan."

Wigan owner Mike Danson said: "Billy Boston was everybody's hero, including my mum's.

"His achievements in rugby league were extraordinary, and his knighthood was a fitting recognition of a career that brought great credit to Wigan and to the game.

"But Billy's legacy was not simply what he achieved. It was the humility with which he carried it. Despite everything he accomplished, he remained a quiet, dignified and deeply respected man.

"He leaves behind an example that will endure for generations. Our thoughts are with his family and those closest to him.

"A great man, and a true Wigan legend. He will be remembered with pride and affection."

In a statement, Wales Rugby League said: "Today, rugby league has lost one of its greatest-ever players, Wales has lost one of its finest sporting sons, and our sport has lost a truly special gentleman."

The WRU also paid tribute, calling Boston "one of the best loved and most iconic figures in the history of Welsh sport".

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy added: "He was, in my view, the greatest rugby league player of all time and one of the nicest people I've ever had the privilege to know."

News.title: Former police officer charged with raping woman while on duty
News.content:
A former police officer allegedly raped and strangled a woman while on duty, according to the policing watchdog.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said ex-constable Rikki Hall had been charged with two counts of rape and one count of non-fatal strangulation.

The 33-year-old is accused of attacking the woman while on duty in Swansea city centre in February 2024.

Hall, who resigned from South Wales Police during the IOPC investigation, has also been charged with possession of a firearm and two counts of misconduct in public office.

He will appear at Bristol Magistrates' Court on Thursday.

The IOPC said its investigation began in February 2024 following a mandatory conduct referral from South Wales Police.

"A substantial file of material was submitted to the Crown Prosecution Service in February 2025 and, following further lines of enquiry being undertaken, charges were authorised by the CPS," it added.

News.title: 'We just want to get home' - dozens stranded in Tunisia after cancelled Belfast flight
News.content:
Dozens of people from Northern Ireland have been left stranded in Tunisia after their EasyJet flight home was cancelled, with the airline telling them it had no other flights available for another 10 days.

One man told BBC News NI he has spent Â£4,000 on travel home for his family-of-five, while another woman, Georgina Doherty, said her and her six children were trying to get home after the death of her mother-in-law.

Others described running out of medication for health issues, while EasyJet were also criticised over a lack of support and communication.

EasyJet has said it is operating an additional direct flight to Belfast on Tuesday night, and that it was "very sorry" for the inconvenience.

The airline said it was "very sorry" for the inconvenience.

BBC News NI understands more than 100 people were booked onto the cancelled flight that was due to leave Enfidha-Hamamet Airport for Belfast International three days ago.

Stuart McCartney, from Dromore, County Down, said he had spent thousands on accommodation and flights to get his family home via a flight to Brussels.

"I'm willing to pay Â£4,000 to get us home, if needs be, and then battle for reimbursement if I have to after that," he said.

"But we shouldn't have to pay. My holiday was a fraction of what I'm paying to get home right now."

McCartney said EasyJet provided two nights of accommodation but then told the family to find alternative accommodation for the rest of the delay.

He said his mother Katherine, who accompanied his wife and children on the trip, relies on heart medication and they have had to keep a close eye on her remaining supply as the delay continued.

An EasyJet spokesperson said they were "very sorry" that the flight had been cancelled and that the company "have been doing everything we can to support Mr McCartney, providing hotel accommodation and meals and we will be reimbursing expenses that may have been incurred".

Georgina Doherty, who is originally from Londonderry but now lives in County Donegal, told BBC News NI the last few days have been an "absolute nightmare" for her family.

Her husband returned home a day before they were due to fly back due to his mother taking ill. She has since died, with Doherty and her six children stranded in Tunisia.

News.title: More than 70,000 social and affordable homes to be built across England over 10 years
News.content:
Ministers have announced where more than 70,000 social and affordable homes will be built in England over the next 10 years as part of an initial allocation of almost Â£10bn in a bid to address the housing crisis.

Funding has been granted to Greater Manchester, the West Midlands, West Yorkshire, South Yorkshire, North East England, and Liverpool. An additional Â£6bn was previously announced for London.

It is the first part of a wider plan to build 300,000 social and affordable homes, under the government's Â£39bn social housebuilding programme.

Housing charities welcomed the news but said it was still not enough to meet demand, while the Conservatives said it was an "unfunded spending commitment".

Social housing provides affordable homes at a low cost, managed by social landlords. It includes affordable rented properties as well as low-cost home ownership, such as shared ownership, and can be provided by local authorities and housing associations.

Earlier this year, before he became prime minister, Andy Burnham had called for the entire Â£39bn affordable housing budget for England to be spent on homes for social rent - which means the cost of the unit is about half that of market rents, and there are strict criteria for who can apply for it.

"I would actually devote all of it to social housing," Burnham told The Social Housing Podcast in May.

But of the new homes announced on Monday, 60% would be for social rent.

Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook told BBC Breakfast he did not accept Burnham had failed to meet his previous commitment, saying the government had taken a "pragmatic approach" and wants to "get money out the door".

He said the next tranche of funding would be more focused on council houses - which are usually also classed as homes for social rent.

It is understood ministers decided against giving councils more of the funding announced in the first tranche because they did not believe councils would be in a position to build the required number of social homes.

News.title: Andrew Tate exaggerates and did not own supercars in photos, his lawyers say
News.content:
Controversial influencer Andrew Tate portrays himself as "uberwealthy" but did not own cars and a yacht featured on his social media and exaggerated his lifestyle for online attention, his legal representatives have said.

Tate and his brother Tristan are currently being held in a Florida jail but are seeking release on bail while they await the outcome of extradition proceedings.

They were arrested last month after British prosecutors unveiled new charges including alleged sexual offences against them, which both men deny.

Prosecutors have argued the Tates are a "flight risk", citing the brothers' past statements about their wealth and influence and having multiple identities to evade the law.

In a legal submission to the court, the brothers' legal representatives said the Tates' business model "depends on online attention".

"The outrageousness of the posts by them and about them is the point. The more hyperbolic and outlandish the post, the more likely it will generate views and likes, which in turn generates income. In short, they are playing a role," it says.

At times Andrew Tate has also exaggerated and used hyperbole for "comedic effect" with no intention to be taken seriously, the submission argues.

"The government alleges that the Tates are a risk of flight based on their social media claims that they are 'self-proclaimed billionaires' who own 'high-end vehicles, private jets, and a custom $50-million-dollar superyacht and have unrestricted access to traditional funds, cryptocurrency, and bitcoin,'" it says.

"But the government has not established these grandiose claims are true," it adds.

News.title: Man jailed for killing student over fake Rolex row
News.content:
At about 17:00 GMT on the night he died, Oladipo left his girlfriend's flat carrying a plastic bag of leftover snacks and was on the phone to her while he walked back to his accommodation nearby to watch football.

But outside the De Montfort University's Innovation Centre, he was met by Dennis who was captured on CCTV walking up and down in the "busy" area.

"It took less than 30 seconds for the two men to come together, to struggle and for the defendant to leave," Osborne told the court.

The court was told Oladipo's girlfriend heard him say "why did you come up and stab me?" over the phone before asking for her to call the ambulance.

A post-mortem examination showed he had suffered six wounds, five to the chest including one which penetrated his heart, and one to his thumb.

Despite being taken to the Leicester Royal Infirmary, he was pronounced dead just over an hour after the stabbing, which took place near the DMU campus.

Giving evidence in his defence on Wednesday, Dennis said he was "fearful" for his life when Oladipo approached him with a knife, adding he was "wrestling" to prevent the 20-year-old from stabbing him.

In cross-examination, prosecutor Jane Osborne KC asked if Dennis knew he had stabbed Oladipo, to which he replied: "I didn't know and I didn't know he was hurt, and I didn't intend to cause any serious harm."

Jurors were shown CCTV footage of Oladipo and Dennis walking towards each other, with Osborne suggesting Dennis used his hands to open a folding knife.

Dennis denied the suggestion he had a knife in his possession, and said he did not leave his accommodation with one.

Addressing Dennis, the prosecutor said there was "bad feeling" between Dennis and Oladipo - and suggested Dennis left his accommodation with a knife "to settle it".

News.title: Burnham refuses to rule out tax rises in autumn Budget
News.content:
Andy Burnham has refused to rule out tax rises in the upcoming autumn Budget, saying he "won't be unrealistic" about the "challenging" state of public finances.

The prime minister said he would take a "careful approach" to the economy, and defended his previously announced cost of living pledges as funded spending commitments.

Burnham became prime minister in July promising to give people breathing space and help with the cost of living, but questions remain over how major policies such as social care reforms will be funded.

Experts have previously warned that he and Chancellor John Healey will have little financial room to manoeuvre in their first Budget on 28 October.

Speaking during his first visit to Ukraine, Burnham said the policies announced so far including capping bus fares at Â£2 and cutting VAT on household electricity bills were "the first steps that I've felt able to make", and were doable because he was able to reprioritise funding from elsewhere.

"I took the decision early on that digital ID wasn't the top priority for now. And so we've reprioritised funding to other priorities," he said in an interview with ITV.

Asked if the public needed to accept some of the new policies would have to be paid for in tax rises, Burnham said they wouldn't necessarily have to accept that.

Pushed on whether he would need to raise taxes to cover spending gaps, he said: "I will always take a careful approach to things. I ran Greater Manchester for 10 years and we ran a very tight ship with rock solid finances.

"Nothing will change as I come into this role as prime minister. I won't take risks with people's jobs or their livelihoods or their family finances.

"I will try to help them in whatever way I can, I have already done some things that will help them."

Burnham previously told the BBC he accepts his earlier announcements aimed at tackling the cost of living are not enough on their own and hinted at further support.

Speaking during his first official overseas visit on Monday, he said while he would do what he could, "I won't be unrealistic and people really need to understand that.

"We are in a challenging position, whatever I do will be carefully thought through, it will be funded and there will be more to come as we go into the autumn."

Last week official figures showed the the government borrowed more than expected in July, despite a record month for income tax receipts.

Inflation also reached a four-month high of 2.9% in July and is expected to rise further due to the ongoing impact of the Iran war, which has hit energy prices and fuel costs.

Experts have warned Burnham and Healey that they need to either raise taxes or cut spending elsewhere as pressure on the public finances has left no room for extra borrowing.

Both the prime minister and chancellor have vowed to stick to the fiscal rules set by former chancellor Rachel Reeves.

The rules are designed to ensure day-to-day spending is funded through tax revenue by the end of the Parliament, and to reduce debt as a proportion of GDP.

Rain Newton-Smith, chief executive of the Confederation of British Industry, said business owners wanted to create opportunities for young people but "the cost of employing people has gone up so much".

"The business leaders I speak to say that the cost of doing business has gone up so much that it's holding them back from creating opportunities," she told the Today programme.

She said targeted support for businesses would create "more growth and more opportunities that saves money for the government and ultimately leads to higher tax receipts".

News.title: Lions v New Zealand LIVE: Latest updates as All Blacks play final tour match after first Test triumph
News.content:
( Reuters )

New Zealand play their final midweek tour fixture in South Africa with confidence high after a statement first Test success over the Springboks in Johannesburg.

The All Blacks return to Ellis Park to take on the Lions a few days on from an excellent 33-16 win at the venue that allowed them to go 1-0 up in the Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry’s series. With three more tough battles with the world champions to come, this game will be a chance for some of those on the fringes to retain their sharpness and push for places, with Dave Rennie likely to need plenty of strength in depth as the back-to-back encounters continue.

Cape Town and the second Test await but the Lions could prove tricky opposition. The United Rugby Championship side are bolstered by a couple of members of the South Africa squad that have been released to feature here, and will hope to provide a stern test for the tourists.

Follow all of the latest from the clash at Ellis Park with our live blog below:

Canada is rolling out a slate of retaliatory trade moves against the U.S. in response to Donald Trump’s latest tariffs after negotiations between the neighboring nations broke down in an escalating trade war.

“Canada must respond,” Canadian Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said Tuesday.

Canada, which imports roughly $272 billion in U.S. goods every year, will double its existing counter-tariffs on American steel and aluminum products to 50 percent, while new tariffs of 15, 25 and 50 percent will be applied to more than $20 billion worth of about 700 U.S. goods, including clothing, furniture, video game consoles and other electronics, among other goods.

The measures are “proportionate, targeted and strategic,” designed to “match dollar for dollar, rate for rate” against Trump’s tariff agenda, Champagne said. The new levies are effective September 8.

Canada’s new levies are “designed primarily to provide protection for Canadian industry impacted by American tariffs” and to “level the playing field” in the face of Trump’s trade war, he said. Officials have stressed that the retaliatory measures are intended to protect workers and industry, not collect revenue; Canada will cushion the economic blow from the latest battle in the trade war with a $5.4 billion package to boost support for impacted workers and businesses.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump has waged a retaliatory trade war with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, whose government announced new ‘targeted’ tariffs on hundreds of American goods to match US levies ( AFP/Getty )

The Trump administration’s 50 percent tariffs on many Canadian products went into effect Saturday after the president laid out last-minute “unfair” and “uneconomic” terms last week, according to Prime Minister Mark Carney.

“We did not choose this conflict, but when our economic integration is used as a weapon rather than the foundation for a win-win partnership, we need to stand up,” Champagne said Tuesday.

Goods subject to the 50 percent counter tariffs include steel and aluminum products that were previously only subject to a 25 percent tax, while furniture and clothing will also face 50 percent levies.

Dairy, appliances, cheese and fish will face 25 percent duties, and a rate of 15 percent will apply to other products including rubber molds and machinery parts, according to Canada officials.

Canada will retain a previous retaliatory 25 percent tariff on American-made cars at 25 percent.

Minister of Industry of Canada Mélanie Joly said some of the targeted tariffs were designed to exert “political pressure,” particularly in states that have supported the president, coming in the critical weeks before midterm elections with the balance of power in Congress — and the fate of Trump’s remaining years in office — at stake.

She did not list the states but said those targeted goods include appliances and “food products.”

“We’re also targeting products that will target states in the U.S.,” she told reporters Tuesday. “And so we’re being wise and strategic to put political pressure, and that’s why we think it’s the right thing to do right now.”

Trump, meanwhile, has commanded Canadian leaders to “fall in line” or face consequences “far WORSE” than already-imposed tariffs, including threatening new 50 percent tariffs on Canadian vehicles, auto parts and steel.

A 50 percent tariff on Canadian vehicle imports would likely debilitate Canadian manufacturers, which export roughly 90 percent of what they build. Trump has also suggested that he could extend those levies to Canadian auto parts.

open image in gallery Canadian officials unveiled a suite of new tariffs on American goods on August 25, including 50 percent counter tariffs on steel and aluminum products and 25 percent duties on dairy, appliances, cheese and fish, among other products, estimated to target more than $20 billion in American goods ( AP )

Ontario Premier Doug Ford unleashed his own vitriol, telling Trump to “kiss my as**.”

“We’re going to go at him full steam,” he said Monday.

In an interview with the Associated Press, Ford said Ronald Reagan himself would be “throwing up” on Trump and “spinning around in his grave” if the former president “knew what was going on.”

Trump responded in a social media post by attacking Ford personally, calling him “the less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother of the late, great, Rob Ford.”

“If you think an insult from him hurts me? Well, bring it on, buddy, I’m ready,” Ford replied.

On Tuesday morning, hours before Canadian officials unveiled new tariffs, Trump threatened to rename Lake Ontario to “Lake America.”

“We’ll always call it Lake Ontario. Period. We’re proud of our Great Lakes,” Joly said during Tuesday’s press conference.

“While all these shenanigans are happening, we’ll just be smart, we’ll be strategic, and we’ll fight back,” she said.

The monumental collection of 76 statues in Suse Lowenstein’s backyard captures the moment she and other women learned their loved ones were killed when Pan Am Flight 103 was blown out of the sky over Lockerbie, Scotland, in 1988.

Each nude, life-size creation represents a mother, wife, sister or other female relative in her darkest grief -- weeping, praying, screaming, collapsing.

“The grief, everything, stays the same, just like this. This is always here,” the 82-year-old artist said, walking through the rust-hued monuments in the New York beach town of Montauk recently. “And so, the feelings don’t go away.”

Lowenstein, whose son, Alex, was aboard Flight 103, is among many who have waited nearly four decades to see the culprits of the bombing — one of the deadliest terrorist attacks against U.S. citizens — face justice in a U.S. courtroom. Now, they'll have to keep waiting.

The terrorism trial of the alleged bombmaker, Abu Agila Mohammad Mas’ud Kheir Al-Marimi, was set to begin Wednesday in Washington, D.C., but was postponed Monday. A judge cited the discovery of new evidence, though she didn't say what that evidence was.

Al-Marimi, a former Libyan intelligence officer who had been imprisoned in Libya for years, is the first to be prosecuted on American soil in connection with the attack on the New York-bound flight, which killed 270 people, a majority of them Americans. Eleven of the dead were on the ground in Lockerbie.

The case had a breakthrough in 2017, when U.S. officials obtained a 2012 interview in which they say that Al-Marimi admitted building the bomb and working with two conspirators to carry out the attack. According to an FBI affidavit, he said the operation was ordered by Libyan intelligence and that the late Libyan leader Moammar Gadhafi thanked the team afterward.

A mother honors her late daughter’s photography dreams

Aphrodite Tsairis, whose daughter, Alexia, perished on Flight 103, had planned to travel to Washington for the start of the trial, along with other family members of victims. She said the delay wasn't surprising.

“From the very beginning, we had to fight adversity,” the 83-year-old central New Jersey resident said Tuesday. "So it is not surprising to hear there are more impediments to justice being carried out.”

Tsairis said the court proceeding was more of “an academic exercise” than an emotional journey, at this stage in her life. She and other family members of victims had attended the 2000 trial in the Netherlands, which resulted in the conviction of one of Al-Marimi's alleged accomplices and the acquittal of another.

“This isn’t about closure,” Tsairis said. “This is more about putting the period at the end of the sentence kind of thing.”

She said she's found solace over the years working with her husband on The Alexia, a grant program supporting documentary photographers and filmmakers at Syracuse University. Their 20-year-old daughter, who had dreams of becoming a documentary photographer, was among the 35 Syracuse students returning from a semester abroad on the ill-fated flight.

“It’s been our survival,” Tsairis says of the grant program and its recipients. “Through them, I know what Alexia would have become.”

A brother believes others should be held accountable

Bert Ammerman, who lost his 36-year-old brother, Thomas, in the bombing, doesn't believe the trial, whenever it happens, should be the end of the story.

The retired school teacher and administrator from New Jersey says he believes other nations were involved and should still be held responsible, even though the Libyan government formally accepted responsibility in 2003 and agreed to pay nearly $3 billion to victims’ families.

“This does not belong in the criminal arena,” said Ammerman, who was founding president of Victims of Pan Am Flight 103, an advocacy group formed by families in the wake of the bombing. “This was an attack on the U.S. This was an act of war.”

Stephanie Bernstein, who lost her husband, Michael, in the attack, said it’s “astonishing” that evidence apparently not known by either side in the case would emerge all these decades later and on the eve of the trial.

“It shows that there is still information out there, so that makes the delay somewhat less difficult to accept,” said the 75-year-old Maryland resident, who is currently vice president of the victims’ advocacy group. “We are hopeful that it will increase our knowledge of what happened.”

Lowenstein's son says his parents ‘more or less died that day' too

Suse Lowenstein’s son, Lucas, hopes whatever new information emerges can finally put to bed any lingering theories.

“You can really go down a rabbit hole in wondering, ‘What did we miss? Is there more?’” he said. “At this point, I feel that they got the right people. I don’t believe there’s more to it.”

The 57-year-old northern New Jersey resident says his approach to life fundamentally changed when he lost his brother. The two had been students together at Syracuse University, just one year apart.

His father, Peter, who had been among the many grieving family members who thrust themselves into a lifetime of seeking justice and airline security reforms, died in 2018.

“My parents more or less died that day,” said Lucas Lowenstein, who named his son in honor of his late brother. “So I knew then -- and know now — that I have to outlive them. I got to be there for them.”

Suse's home is a living monument to grief and loss

Out in Montauk, some 100 miles (160 kilometers) east of Manhattan, Suse Lowenstein has tried to stay out of the twists and turns of the criminal case. Instead, she finds peace among the constant reminders of what was lost on Dec. 21, 1988.

Her son Alex's bright red jacket rests on a hook by the door of her art studio. Slightly singed and torn, the coat was recovered amid the mangled wreckage and carefully cleaned by residents of Lockerbie, like so many other possessions returned to grieving families. Lowenstein says she dons it whenever she does welding work.

On a wall nearby, a large framed photo captures the surf-loving Alex standing joyfully on a bluff high above the crashing waves, arms outstretched, his hair blowing in the breeze.

Outside, two white statues depicting Alex and Lucas as young boys sit side-by-side at the edge of a swimming pool, their feet dipping in the clear water.

And in a shaded corner of the yard stands “Dark Elegy,” Lowenstein’s life’s work. The sculptor represented herself in two of the statues — one curled up in pain and another standing in front of it, arms outstretched.

“First, I created myself in the position that my body took when the phone call came,” she explained. “Then I created myself again, basically holding myself up and staying alive.”

Lowenstein says she shares the frustration at the latest delay but is confident Al-Marimi will ultimately be found guilty. She prays the elderly defendant lives long enough to meet his fate.

“I hope they convict him and put him into the worst prison that the Americans have,” Lowenstein said.
