The group includes private lenders Kapital Bank and PASHA Bank. Banks linked to the family control a significant share of Azerbaijan’s banking-sector assets — more than 40%, according to some estimates. SOCAR: Azerbaijan’s state oil company is also entering Uzbekistan’s retail fuel market and plans to establish a network of filling stations there. At the same time, the company plans to cooperate with BP and Uzbekneftegaz on the Ustyurt field. SOCAR has also faced questions over transparency in the past, including in connection with the Azerbaijani Laundromat scandal.

Azerbaijan’s state oil company is also entering Uzbekistan’s retail fuel market and plans to establish a network of filling stations there. At the same time, the company plans to cooperate with BP and Uzbekneftegaz on the Ustyurt field. SOCAR has also faced questions over transparency in the past, including in connection with the Azerbaijani Laundromat scandal. Other projects: Other businesses entering the Uzbek market include the Matanat-A gypsum plant, Landau STEAM schools, the Sur gold and silver processing plant, Gold Fresh Fruits orchards, the Baku City residential complex and other projects. Some are being implemented as public-private partnerships.

Statements by the two presidents

President Ilham Aliyev said in a statement to the press that relations between the two countries were built “on a very solid foundation, both spiritually and materially”. He said the range of projects under discussion in energy, transport, investment, tourism, mining, automotive manufacturing, agriculture, processing and banking gave the cooperation an “unprecedented character”.

Aliyev said that on every visit he was struck by the rapid development of Tashkent and Uzbekistan as a whole. He said increasing bilateral trade to $1bn was “no longer a dream of the distant future, but a target that can be achieved within a few years”. He also highlighted Mirziyoyev’s particular role in attracting investment to Karabakh and invited him to make a state visit to Azerbaijan at a time convenient to him.

Shavkat Mirziyoyev described Aliyev’s visit as a “historic event”, saying the “Treaty on Eternal Friendship” was evidence of this and that the provisions on strategic partnership and alliance were being backed up by concrete action. In his remarks, he highlighted a threefold increase in bilateral trade over the past five years, the goal of raising it to $1bn, the joint development of the Middle Corridor, and the idea of creating a separate Azerbaijani-Uzbek corridor across the Caspian Sea with a single operator.

Mirziyoyev also said the two countries spoke “with one voice” on the international stage. He described Azerbaijan’s full participation in the consultative meetings of Central Asian heads of state as a historic step and praised Aliyev’s policy of restoring Azerbaijan’s territorial integrity, as well as the meeting in Washington and the declaration signed there.

Hikmet Hajiyev, a representative of the Azerbaijani presidential administration, said before and during the visit that relations between the two countries had reached a new level: moving from strategic partnership to alliance and then to “eternal friendship”. He said this was the first such step in the history of Azerbaijani diplomacy. According to Hajiyev, the “eternal friendship” that had already existed de facto between the two peoples had now been formally enshrined at the political level as well.

World.title: “When the state serves an oligarch, villages and cities empty out.” Video podcast “Protests in Georgia”
World.content:
Video podcast “Protests in Georgia”

The traditional pro-European “Saturday march” in Tbilisi on August 22 was dedicated to Georgian citizens who have left the country in search of work and better opportunities.

Participants said the growing emigration is driven by the policies of the ruling Georgian Dream party, which they say have pushed the country away from the European integration path enshrined in the Constitution.

Many blame the party’s founder and honorary chairman, oligarch Bidzina Ivanishvili, personally.

“Villages and cities are emptying out when the state serves Ivanishvili” — this was the central message of the march, reflected in the slogans and statements by speakers.

Organisers announced that throughout September, the traditional “Saturday marches” will be held in support of Georgian emigrants.

For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society. Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms. For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years. To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

News in Georgia

World.title: Armenia’s new parliament: balance of power, tools of government and opposition’s dead end
World.content:
Balance of power in Armenia’s new parliament

The parliamentary election results in Armenia have confirmed the continuity of the country’s political system while exposing deep structural contradictions. Political competition has shifted decisively towards intense polarisation. The National Assembly risks turning into little more than a platform for mutual accusations resembling a television talk show, rather than the country’s highest legislative body.

Political analyst Alexander Iskandaryan’s assessment

Continuity of the system, limits of influence and a fragmented opposition

“The new National Assembly has retained the key feature of its predecessor. The Constitution allows the ruling Civil Contract party to make almost any decision on its own, except on issues that require a constitutional majority. The two opposition factions — former president Robert Kocharyan’s Armenia Alliance and businessman Samvel Karapetyan’s Strong Armenia — have access to the media and the parliamentary platform, and can openly express their views and criticise the government. However, they have no real leverage over current policy.

The opposition forces have undergone a reshuffle. In the eighth National Assembly, Kocharyan’s faction held the largest number of seats. In the new parliament, however, it is the smaller of the two opposition factions. They are also unlikely to build a stable coalition or an “umbrella” structure. Because of their different origins and the lack of a practical basis for cooperation, even if they unite, they will not secure 50% of the seats needed to take the initiative. A long-term alliance is impossible. In 35 years of the Third Republic, the opposition has never managed to produce a successful example of unity. The minority is therefore left with little more than keeping the protest movement alive.”

Legitimacy, voters and the government’s narratives

“The ruling party has significant external legitimacy. This includes recognition of the election results by the US, EU, Turkey and Azerbaijan, as well as Russia’s refusal to withhold recognition from Nikol Pashinyan. The ruling force also relies on support from the bureaucracy. In fact, bureaucratic legitimacy has grown stronger. Civil servants clearly understand their ties to the political leadership and recognise the risks that a change of elites could bring.

At the same time, the government’s social legitimacy remains low. Kocharyan won 10% despite his high negative rating, while Karapetyan’s party, hastily assembled over six months with its leader under arrest, won a quarter of the vote despite high turnout. This is a serious signal of the level of public dissatisfaction.

Realising that its support will not grow, the government abandoned any real ideology. Political strategists pragmatically discarded the “high-minded Yerevan intelligentsia”, which would not have voted for the government anyway and would not have gone to the polls. Instead, they focused on their target audience: residents of small towns and villages with lower levels of education, young people and older generations.

To maintain control, the government uses several narratives:

“Peace versus war” — portraying opponents as the “party of war” and frightening voters with the prospect that an opposition victory would lead to a new war in September.

“Democrats versus oligarchs” — selectively labelling businesses. Wealthy entrepreneurs who support the government are simply called “businessmen”, while any affluent opponents are automatically branded “oligarchs”.

“Europe versus Russia” — systematically linking the entire opposition to Moscow. Karapetyan is portrayed this way because he came from Russia, Gagik Tsarukyan because of his ties to Belarus, and Kocharyan as Putin’s personal friend.

Accusing voters of supporting the opposition solely for money. This new level of polarisation has emerged in official statements by the authorities.”

The government’s geopolitical narrative and the opposition’s dead end

“The government’s anti-Russian discourse found fertile ground. These sentiments had been developing for years, and the events of 2020 and 2023 — the war in Karabakh, followed by the exodus of the entire Armenian population from Nagorno-Karabakh — only strengthened them.

At the same time, people across the post-Soviet space have traditionally associated the word “European” with quality and development: European healthcare, European education, European cars and so on. The government has effectively exploited this perception. Direct public support for Pashinyan from senior US officials, up to and including the US president, also played an important role.

The opposition has found itself in a strategic dead end. It cannot openly say “we are pro-Russian” or “we are not pro-Russian”. Unable to reject the geopolitical trend that enjoys broad public support, opposition parties have had to adapt and repeat that they are “also in favour of cooperation with Europe, but for a more carefully calibrated policy”.

Personal attacks instead of alternative programmes

“Instead of substantive work, the opposition is sliding into negative rhetoric and personal attacks: who is corrupt, who got their wife a job, who owns which flat and who once “didn’t even have a washing machine”. Armenian society knows perfectly well how the bureaucratic hierarchy works, so such “exposés” do not work. All these scandals only play into the government’s hands, allowing it to say: “Look who we have to work with in parliament.”

A constructive alternative would be to develop concrete programmes in different areas — healthcare, pensions, the economy, the army and so on. Even if the ruling majority rejects, say, 15 such professional programmes in a row, a systematic effort to offer solutions will eventually resonate with society. For now, trolling has replaced politics.”

Real state priorities: security, energy and meritocracy

“While parliament is busy trolling, the country’s key problems remain unresolved. One of them is security.

It is wrong to call the situation with Azerbaijan peace. You can see what real peace looks like on the border with Georgia, for example: people can cross freely using an ID card, while there are no transport corridors, European observers, military guards or concrete walls, even though 30% of the border remains undelimited. With Baku, however, there is only a state of “no war”. That is far from peace. At the same time, Azerbaijan is rapidly expanding its military capabilities in every sphere, including its air force.

Armenia needs to make foreign policy decisions and find ways to overcome the energy crisis.

Relations with all four neighbours — Russia, Turkey, Azerbaijan and Iran — are in crisis. Meanwhile, the Armenian-American TRIPP “Trump Route” project — a transit route through Armenia — remains little more than a political narrative. At the same time, launching new facilities, such as an AI data centre in Hrazdan, could create an acute electricity shortage that talk of American small modular nuclear reactors alone cannot solve.

In the Armenian city of Hrazdan, Firebird AI’s artificial intelligence factory has begun operations. The facility is the largest AI data centre in the region. The first phase of the project, worth more than $500 million, uses advanced NVIDIA accelerators and server equipment from leading global manufacturers. Some experts believe the factory’s launch could put additional pressure on the country’s energy system. (firebird.ai)

The state needs a competent administration to overcome these challenges.

The country needs to embrace meritocracy, appointing people based on competence rather than loyalty.

Finally, the country’s leadership needs to reconsider its attitude towards citizens.

Nikol Pashinyan is the prime minister of all Armenians, not just the voters of Civil Contract. The claim that people could only have voted against the government in exchange for money is false and toxic. The government now faces a vast array of real problems. Its first task is to recognise the scale of those challenges and start addressing them.

Balance of power in Armenia’s new parliament

World.title: Anea the raccoon’s favourite activity at Tbilisi Zoo – video
World.content:
Anea the raccoon at Tbilisi Zoo

Raccoons love water. You can often see them swimming, wetting their fur or carefully washing their paws. Anea, a resident of Tbilisi Zoo, is no exception.

On hot days, Anea particularly enjoys dipping her paws in water and having a cool shower. So her keepers set up an improvised shower in her enclosure, which, as you can see in the video below, delighted her.

There is a metal container in her enclosure for drinking water, but who says she cannot take a bath in it too? Despite its small size, Anea fits perfectly inside, happily splashes around in the water and uses it to escape the summer heat. After noticing the raccoon’s love of bathing, her keepers have already ordered a bigger “bath”.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status.



The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo.



We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Anea the raccoon at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Tajikistan, Belarus discuss new prospects for bilateral cooperation
World.content:
Photo: Press Service of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Tajikistan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 25. Tajikistan and Belarus discussed prospects for developing bilateral cooperation.

This was announced in a report published by the press service of the Tajik MFA, following the meeting between Minister Sirojiddin Muhriddin and newly appointed Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of Belarus to Tajikistan Alexander Khudoleyev.

The meeting between the minister and the newly appointed ambassador was held on the occasion of the formal presentation of copies of the ambassador’s credentials.

"During the meeting, the current state and prospects for bilateral cooperation between Tajikistan and Belarus were discussed," the statement said.

The Minister of Foreign Affairs wished the new Ambassador of Belarus success in his diplomatic activities in Tajikistan.

Meanwhile, Tajikistan and Belarus maintain diplomatic relations and cooperate through bilateral and multilateral frameworks. Their cooperation covers areas including trade and economic relations, agriculture, industry, education, and humanitarian ties, while the two countries also maintain regular political contacts.

World.title: Azerbaijan facilitates transit of new Russian shipment to Armenia
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 25. Another shipment from Russia to Armenia has been delivered via Azerbaijan.

On August 25, 14 railcars of wheat weighing 976 metric tons and 1 railcar of lumber weighing 65 metric tons were dispatched from the Bilajari station in Boyuk-Kesik.

To date, more than 50,000 metric tons of grain, about 9,000 metric tons of fertilizer, 1,414 metric tons of propane, 133 metric tons of aluminum, 1,114 metric tons of coal, and 67 metric tons of lumber have been shipped from Russia to Armenia via Azerbaijan.

In addition, approximately 15,000 metric tons of diesel fuel and about 5,000 metric tons of RON-92 and RON-95 gasoline have been exported from Azerbaijan to Armenia to date.

World.title: Kazakhstan strengthens Caspian Sea emergency fleet with new vessel
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 25. A delegation from Kazakhstan's Ministry of Emergency Situations, together with Tengiz Zhasagy, has completed the acceptance of a new DAMEN Fast Crew Supplier 2710 vessel.

This was announced by the press service of the Ministry of Emergency Situations.

Built by DAMEN Workboats at its production facility in Kuressaare, Estonia, the vessel is designed for search-and-rescue and emergency response operations, oil spill response, rapid intervention during emergencies, and ensuring navigational safety in Kazakhstan's sector of the Caspian Sea.

The vessel's arrival comes as the Caspian Sea continues to experience declining water levels and increasingly shallow conditions in some areas. Changes in navigation conditions increase the risk of vessels running aground and other incidents that could threaten lives and cause environmental damage.

"The new vessel will allow Kazakhstan's rescuers to reach the scene of an incident faster, provide timely assistance to people in distress and respond more effectively to the consequences of accidents," the ministry said.

The DAMEN Fast Crew Supplier 2710 is expected to strengthen the operational capabilities of Kazakhstan's emergency fleet, enabling faster response to maritime incidents and supporting search-and-rescue and environmental protection operations.

World.title: Uzbekistan marks its 35th Independence anniversary with 163 new projects
World.content:
Photo: The Press service of the President of Uzbekistan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 25. As part of the celebrations marking the 35th anniversary of independence, Uzbekistan has commissioned 72 major industrial and service facilities, as well as 91 social infrastructure projects across the country.

This was reflected in the statement by the press service of the Uzbek president.

According to the statement, Mirziyoyev took part in a ceremony marking the commissioning of new facilities and stated that over the past decade, Uzbekistan has laid the foundation for what he called a new era of national development.

Furthermore, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev emphasized that investment, industrial diversification, and job creation are key factors in the country’s economic transformation.

“The last 10 years will forever be written into the history of our country as a period of laying the foundation for a new era of revival — the Third Renaissance,” Mirziyoyev said.

According to the president, Uzbekistan’s economy has grown more than 2.5 times over the past decade, while the country has attracted $160 billion in foreign investment and commissioned 2,163 major industrial facilities worth a combined $76 billion. Nearly 6 million permanent jobs have been created during the period.

Mirziyoyev stated that the country was moving away from an economy dependent on raw-material exports toward one focused on deeper processing and higher-value products.

“We are moving from a country oriented toward exporting raw materials to an economy capable of bringing finished products to global markets through deep-processing value chains,” he said.

The projects commissioned Tuesday have a combined value of nearly 50 trillion soums (about $4.2 billion) and are expected to create 15,000 jobs and generate an additional 1 trillion soums (around $84.9 million) in annual budget revenues.

The new facilities span energy, agriculture, food processing, metallurgy, automotive manufacturing, electrical equipment, construction materials, mining and textiles.

Energy projects include 1,573 megawatts of new generating capacity in Syrdarya region, a 200-MW wind farm and 100-MW energy storage system in Karakalpakstan, and renewable facilities in Navoi region expected to generate 657 million kilowatt-hours annually.

The ceremony also highlighted major investments in education and healthcare. Among the 91 social facilities are 36 kindergartens, 43 schools, seven higher education institutions and three hospitals.

The new University of New Uzbekistan complex in Tashkent covers 10 hectares and can accommodate 7,000 students. A National Library with 30,000 square meters of space was also commissioned.

Mirziyoyev stressed that the value of the projects should not be measured solely by investment and export figures.

“Every investment you make strengthens the foundation of Uzbekistan’s future. Every job you create contributes to the well-being of families,” he said.

The president officially commissioned the projects by pressing a symbolic button at the end of the ceremony.

World.title: Uzbekistan, Mongolia explore regional connectivity via CKU railway
World.content:
Photo: the Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade of Uzbekistan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 25. Uzbekistan and Mongolia are exploring opportunities to expand trade and transportation ties through the “China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan” railway, which could open up new opportunities for strengthening ties with Central Asia and the South Caucasus.

This was reflected in the statement by the Uzbek Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade, following a meeting between officials of the Ministry of Investment and Dulguun Damdin-Od, executive director of the International Think Tank for Landlocked Developing Countries.

According to the Ministry, in the course of the meeting, the sides reviewed prospects for expanding trade, economic, transport and logistics cooperation between the two countries. Bilateral trade reached $51.8 million in 2025, while a business forum held in May brought together more than 70 companies from Uzbekistan and Mongolia.

Particular attention was given to developing high value-added production, building resilient supply chains, opening new international transport routes, simplifying trade procedures and expanding the digitalization of cross-border processes.

The China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway was highlighted as a potential driver of greater regional connectivity. Once implemented, the project could provide Mongolia with additional intermodal transport options linking its markets with Uzbekistan, other Central Asian countries and the South Caucasus.

“The China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway can create additional opportunities for Mongolia to develop intermodal transport links with Uzbekistan and broader regional markets,” the sides noted during the meeting.

The discussions reflect efforts by the two landlocked countries to diversify trade routes and improve connectivity amid growing interest in regional transport corridors.

The sides also agreed to cooperate in preparing for and organizing the 25th CAREC Ministerial Conference, scheduled to take place in Ulaanbaatar in October.

The conference is expected to provide another platform for Uzbekistan and Mongolia to advance discussions on trade facilitation, regional connectivity and transport cooperation.

World.title: Thousands of Rohingya refugees protest camp conditions and plead to return home
World.content:
Tens of thousands of Rohingya refugees have protested over dire conditions in their Bangladesh camps, calling on the international community to help them return home to Myanmar.

But the United Nations has warned the already dire human rights situation in Myanmar has plunged to a "new low", denouncing the "ever-worsening brutal abuse" of Rohingya people in the country.

More than 1.2 million Rohingya refugees currently live in about 30 overcrowded camps in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar, the world's largest refugee settlement, after fleeing Myanmar.

Children make up more than half the population of the camps.

Save the Children's Golam Mostofa said "an entire generation of children is growing up in exile" with conditions deteriorating and food rationed.

"Yet instead of seeing progress towards safety, rights and a lasting solution, families are facing worsening hunger, fewer opportunities and deepening uncertainty about their future," he said.

One in three refugees is expected to face "crisis" hunger levels or worse between September and December, according to Save the Children.

Tens of thousands of Rohingyas refugees have protested against the dire conditions in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar, the world's largest refugee settlement. (AP: Abdul Goni)

As tens of thousands protested the conditions inside the camp on Tuesday, many held placards, some reading "Justice for Rohingya, Hope is Home" and "Timely justice is our right".

Rohingya people adjust to life in Australia The Rohingya, a Muslim ethnic group, have suffered killings, forced evictions and other atrocities.

The United Council of Rohingya (UCR)'s president Sayed Ullah said most were desperate to return home.

"We can't keep waiting for the international community to facilitate our return," he said.

"We will do whatever it takes to ensure our safe return home."

The 2017 Myanmar crackdown, which saw Rohingya villages burned and civilians killed, is the subject of a genocide case at the UN's top court in The Hague.

UN report finds Myanmar's military has 'deepened' suffering for civilians

Over the past five years, more than 100,000 people are believed to have been killed across all sides as the military battles both pro-democracy and ethnic minority rebels.

The UN report released on Tuesday found the military's "persistent quest for control and legitimacy has only deepened the suffering and the multiple life-threatening protection and humanitarian concerns civilians face".

"This report depicts a picture of suffering, misery, and cruelty on multiple levels and across the country that is heartbreaking," UN rights chief Volker Turk said in a statement.

"I call on all states, companies and investors to undertake serious soul-searching with respect to their actions — or inaction — to ask: is this fair and just for the people of Myanmar?"

Refugees want to return home

The United Council of Rohingya said it organised the rally to "remember the atrocities committed" and highlight the "ongoing humanitarian crisis". (AP: Abdul Goni)

Moulovi Abdus Salam arrived in Bangladesh last year after he said his family fled gunmen who "raped our women, killed my brothers and looted my shop".

Yet the 41-year-old said life in Bangladesh had brought new hardships, with food supplies covering "a maximum of 20 days".

"We don't want the life of a refugee," he said.

" My request to the international community is to create the conditions for us to return home. "

How two boats with 500 people disappeared almost without trace The disappearance of two boats carrying more than 500 Rohingya asylum seekers off the coast of Myanmar in recent weeks brings the number of people reported lost at sea in the region this year to more than 800.

Some have attempted dangerous sea journeys in growing desperation to flee the camps.

Bangladeshi authorities have said they are already overstretched and have called for the dignified return of the Rohingya to their homeland.

In a joint statement published by the British High Commission in Bangladesh, diplomatic missions in the country said the conditions in Myanmar did not allow for safe repatriation of the refugees.

"Rohingya refugees have a right to return to their homes in Myanmar," the statement said.

"Regrettably, conflict is escalating across Rakhine and humanitarian need is rising.

Deepening insecurity, airstrikes on civilian infrastructure and the Myanmar authorities' blockades on aid and trade are worsening the humanitarian crisis."

AFP

World.title: Ghislaine Maxwell loses bid to overturn sex trafficking conviction
World.content:
A US federal judge has rejected a bid by Ghislaine Maxwell, a key accomplice of notorious sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, to throw out her conviction on sex trafficking charges.

Maxwell, 64, has been sentenced to 20 years in prison and is the only person convicted of a crime in connection with Epstein, who died in a New York jail cell in 2019 while awaiting his own trial.

In his ruling on Tuesday, local time, Judge Paul Engelmayer said that Maxwell's claims that her constitutional rights at trial and sentencing were violated "are all meritless and all or almost all are frivolous."

Maxwell was convicted in 2021 of supplying underage girls to Epstein, whose ties to powerful business executives, politicians, celebrities and academics have fuelled years of scrutiny and conspiracy theories.

Ghislaine Maxwell remains the only person ever convicted in relation to Jeffrey Epstein. (US Justice Department via Reuters)

Under a new law passed last year, US President Donald Trump's administration has released vast troves of investigative files relating to Epstein, drawing huge public attention to the case.

High-profile figures including Britain's former prince Andrew have been publicly disgraced for their associations with Epstein.

In February, Maxwell was subpoenaed by the House Oversight Committee to discuss her relations with Epstein but refused to answer any questions. Her lawyer stated she would only speak if Trump granted her clemency.

The US Supreme Court last October declined to hear an appeal by Maxwell of her sex trafficking conviction.

Trump, who also had a years-long relationship with Epstein, initially opposed releasing the so-called Epstein files, prompting accusations of a cover-up that dogged his first year back in office.

The Republican has denied any link to Epstein's crimes.

AFP

World.title: Small French village 'bombed by nature' as tornado barrels through
World.content:
A tornado of rare intensity has devastated a village in southern France, causing widespread destruction and leaving residents in shock, with the mayor describing the aftermath as resembling "wartime".

The tornado, which swept through the Aude department late Monday afternoon, local time, hit the small village of Pomas hardest, bringing down walls, tearing off roofs, and uprooting trees.

A tornado moves through Preixan, France, August 24, 2026, in this screengrab obtained from a social media. (Guillaume Noe via Reuters)

Thirty-nine people were injured, including two severely, and 17 people were hospitalised.

Herve Gine, the mayor of Pomas, which is home to around a thousand people, said he had the feeling of living through "a wartime situation".

"We were bombed by nature," he said.

"People are in shock," he said, adding that some "have lost everything".

"The nursery school is gone … We no longer have a school, we no longer have a town hall."

Mr Gine said it was a "miracle" no one died, estimating there could have been several dozen fatalities.

The village's narrow streets testified to the tornado's violence, with debris everywhere, uprooted trees, roof tiles littering the ground, cars overturned, and homes left with shattered windows and torn-off shutters.

'Rare intensity'

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said on X the tornado was "of rare intensity", while Marie-Helene Bouissac, the regional deputy prefect, said it was "an exceptional and highly traumatic event".

Of the village's 476 homes, around 300 were damaged, said the mayor, adding the extent of the destruction was so severe that much of the village would have to be rebuilt.

Local authorities are expressing their relief and amazement that no one died. (Reuters: Manon Cruz)

By early Tuesday, 7,250 households across the Languedoc-Roussillon region were without power including 1,600 in Aude, said grid operator Enedis.

Under clear skies, roofs ripped apart by the storm had been covered with blue and green plastic tarpaulins, an AFP journalist saw.

Nearby fields and vineyards were littered with broken deckchairs, scraps of fibreglass insulation and pieces of wire fencing ripped apart by the fierce winds.

Emergency crews worked throughout the night while local residents tried to salvage what they could.

Firefighters, assisted by a canine search unit, searched the site for possible victims.

"Search and inspection operations are still under way, involving 75 firefighters supported by specialist reinforcement teams," the prefecture said.

'Kids are traumatised'

Overnight, some locals were accommodated in the community hall, which had been converted into a temporary shelter. Others stayed with friends and relatives, officials said.

At a police checkpoint, relatives waited for permission to enter the affected area, bringing supplies or offering assistance.

A castle was among the buldings damaged by the storm. (Reuters: Manon Cruz)

Jose Gomes, a resident of the nearby village of Trebes, said a friend's house had collapsed.

"He was inside, he suffered a head injury and broke three or four ribs," he added. "He got out of hospital this morning."

Abdallah Wakkas, the grandfather of two children aged 13 and 17, said the teenagers were shaken.

"Nothing happened at their house, but the kids are a bit traumatised because their grandmother's roof was torn off," he said.

France sees several dozen tornadoes of varying intensity each year, according to weather agency Meteo-France.

This summer France has endured three heatwaves, registering a record 52 days of heat intensified by climate change. The intense weather conditions have sparked droughts, wildfires and a record number of rockfalls in the Alps.

The impact of global warming on the frequency and intensity of tornadoes is unclear, according to international scientists.

AFP

World.title: Chinese artist jailed over satirical works of ex-leader Mao Zedong
World.content:
A Chinese artist has been sentenced to three years in prison for “infringing upon the reputation of heroes” over his satirical works of art, prompting international condemnation and calls for his immediate release.

Gao Zhen was part of an artistic duo known internationally as the Gao Brothers, whose works included statues of China's former leader Mao Zedong.

The 70-year-old was living and working in the United States but was arrested while visiting family in China in August 2024 and has been in official custody since.

But on Tuesday he was sentenced by the Sanhei People's Court court, according to his wife, Zhao Yaliang.

"We feel outraged," she told Reuters.

"Ever since I learned of the verdict, I haven't been able to recover from it.

"It's devastating."

Chinese artists, the Gao Brothers, with some of their "Miss Mao" pieces in their Beijing studio in 2007. (Reuters: David Gray)

Satirical work featured former Chinese leader Mao Zedong

The charges against Gao relate to artistic works that China's authorities claim insulted revolutionary figures, including a 2009 statue called Mao’s Guilt, which shows the former leader and founder of modern China as kneeling in repentance.

Another prominent piece in the series called Miss Mao, shows a caricatured version of Mao with breasts and an engorged nose.

Amnesty International's China Director Sarah Brooks said this case was designed to "illustrate the authorities' determination to deter others from engaging in independent artistic expression".

"No artist should face criminal punishment for creating work that challenges official narratives or encourages critical reflection on history," she said.

"This trial demonstrates how broadly worded and politically motivated laws are used — and worse, in this case, used retroactively — to silence artists, activists and other individuals who dare to express views that differ from those of the Chinese government.

"The Chinese authorities must repeal the law on heroes and martyrs unless they can ensure that it is in line with international human rights standards and must cease criminalising peaceful expression and artistic creation."

Art from the "Miss Mao" series. (Reuters: David Gray)

Gao retrospectively charged under 2021 laws

Gao was charged under China's "Law on the Protection of Heroes and Martyrs", which came into effect in 2018 and was strengthened in 2021.

In this case, the law has been applied retrospectively for Gao's artworks made between 2005 and 2009.

The ​law has previously been used to prosecute individuals accused of insulting members of the military who died in the line of duty, as well as historical figures.

Diplomats had been barred entry to the trial, according to Gao's wife, who learned of the verdict through his lawyer.

She and her son, a US citizen, have also been blocked from leaving China since her husband's detention two years ago.

Shane Yi, a researcher at Chinese Human Rights Defenders, described the sentence as "a very clear case of a violation of a person's freedom of expression".

"The court has now sentenced him to three years … for artwork he made as far back as 2005, some 16 years before the law he was charged under even existed," he said.

"The only outcome that respects Gao Zhen's rights is his immediate, unconditional release.

"By applying a law retroactively and holding a closed-door trial that shut out even his own family, Chinese authorities have shown exactly how little due process they're willing to give."

The Gao Brothers, whose works addressed themes of authoritarianism and censorship, became famous in a time of relative openness in China and were exhibited both inside the country and abroad.

Reuters/AP

World.title: eHarmony misled Australians over 'free' subscriptions, court rules
World.content:
Users of eHarmony's website and app, the fourth largest of its kind in Australia, were misled with fake free dating services and then forced to pay, the Federal Court of Australia has found.

Users of its free basic membership were unable to talk to other single people online without paying, the court found.

Those who paid for a one-month premium membership were then charged for a six-month subscription, had to pay hidden and additional mandatory fees and were unable to cancel payments that automatically renewed, even after profiles were deleted.

"Try before you buy — and no pressure to sign up," a message on the free dating page read.

"We love our site and want you to enjoy it too, which is why we encourage you to 

Users of eHarmony's free basic membership were unable to talk to other single people online without paying, the court found. (Screenshot)

It was a confusing statement, Justice Christopher Horan said on Tuesday when he found the company deceived its Australian customer base.

"I consider that such an assumption or conclusion was erroneous. Accordingly, the conduct was misleading or deceptive," he said.

"The one-month representation amounted to conduct that was liable to mislead the public.

"I accept the ACCC's submission that it was not possible to use the eHarmony Platform as a Basic member, free of charge, to 'date' other members by engaging in ongoing communications for the purposes of developing a romantic relationship."

The court found about 1.3 million users from Australia registered for a basic membership between 2019 and 2024.

One user who gave evidence to the court — and cannot be named for legal reasons — signed up for a six-month membership at a one-time discounted payment of $155.64, but deleted her profile two months later after failing to meet anyone.

The court will decide on penalties and consumer redress at a later date. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

When the six-month period expired, eHarmony renewed her subscription and billed her credit card $478.80.

She told eHarmony she didn't wish to continue her subscription and cancelled her credit card when the platform refused her request.

The company, which refers to itself as "the No.1 trusted dating app" referred the woman to a debt collection agency.

The proceedings were brought before the federal court after the consumer watchdog became aware of the repeated pattern.

The ACCC received hundreds of complaints from consumers, commissioner Luke Woodward said.

"Dating platforms are an important part of Australians' social lives,'' he said on Tuesday.

"Many people use them to meet others and form valuable connections.

"Consumers were not adequately informed about their memberships' duration or that the membership would automatically renew, including, for many, at a much higher price."

The court will decide on penalties and consumer redress at a later date.

eHarmony has been contacted for comment.

AAP

World.title: Lockerbie bombing trial delayed after new evidence discovered
World.content:
A US judge has postponed the trial of the man authorities allege built the bomb that blew New York-bound Pan Am flight 103 out of the sky over Lockerbie, Scotland, killing 270 people in 1988.

Jury selection had been scheduled to begin on Wednesday, local time, in the trial of Abu Agila Mohammad Mas'ud Kheir Al-Marimi, a Libyan intelligence operative who prosecutors allege once confessed to his role in the 1988 bombing.

In the decision to postpone the trial, US District Judge Dabney Friedrich cited the discovery of new evidence that defence attorneys want to examine.

The judge said "the newly discovered evidence, as well as evidence located in other countries" and "the need for the defence to determine how best to defend this case" made her reach the decision.

Abu Agila Mohammad Masud Kheir Al-Marimi is accused of making the bomb that blew up Pan Am flight 103 over Lockerbie. (Reuters/Alexandria, VA Sheriff's Office)

Judge Friedrich did not schedule a new trial date but set a court hearing on September 1 to discuss next steps.

Mr Mas'ud, now in his mid-70s, has pleaded not guilty to two criminal charges related to the destruction of the aircraft resulting in death and faces a maximum of life in prison if convicted.

The Boeing 747 exploded minutes after take-off from London on December 21, 1988, killing all 259 people on board, including 190 Americans, and 11 people on the ground in Scotland.

Loading...

The bombing made former Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, whose government accepted responsibility for the attack in 2003, an international pariah.

Mr Mas'ud has denied wrongdoing and his lawyers have challenged the credibility of evidence gathered by prosecutors, including Mr Mas'ud's alleged confession to a Libyan police officer in 2012, a year after rebel forces toppled Gaddafi's government.

Mr Mas'ud's trial in Washington DC federal court has been delayed by years of legal wrangling over the alleged confession and other issues that have exposed the complexities of a US prosecution over a decades-old attack in Britain with crucial evidence gathered in Libya.

Mr Mas'ud, who was arrested in Libya and brought to the US in 2022, is accused of building a time-delayed bomb that was packed into a suitcase and placed in checked baggage in Malta.

The explosive-laden suitcase eventually made its way to London Heathrow Airport, where it was stored in the hold of Pan Am flight 103.

Reuters

World.title: Israeli Knesset member vandalises Palestinian memorial in West Bank
World.content:
A right wing Israeli politician has recorded himself taking a sledgehammer to a Palestinian memorial in the occupied West Bank, after being escorted into the village by Israeli soldiers.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) accused Zvi Sukkot of having "acted deceptively and manipulatively" in requesting its protection at the site, confirming it diverted resources to accompany Mr Sukkot only for him to carry out the vandalism.

The 35-year-old member of the Knesset posted video of his attempt to destroy the stone memorial in the town of Madama, south of the city of Nablus, arguing it was a "terror monument".

"Every child who sees a giant monument every day that glorifies Jewish murderers, dreams of being a terrorist," he said on social media.

"There is no place for support for terror in the State of Israel!"

Loading...

Israel's occupation of the West Bank has been deemed unlawful by the International Court of Justice, in an advisory opinion published in 2024.

Video of the incident from witnesses to the vandalism had already spread on social media by the time Mr Sukkot posted his own.

Those videos show soldiers watching on as Israeli settlers hit the monument, which memorialises Palestinians killed over decades, with a military vehicle parked nearby.

In a statement, the IDF said it had received an application for protection from Mr Sukkot earlier in August ahead of a tour of three West Bank villages.

"Contrary to the agreed-upon coordination, the participants acted deceptively and manipulatively, without authorisation, departing entirely from the approved framework, and began demolishing one of the monuments in Madama," it said.

"Upon identifying what was taking place, the soldiers reported the incident to their commanders, who instructed them to stop the activity, and the participants were quickly escorted out of the village.

"IDF soldiers assigned to operational missions in the area were diverted to this task and placed at unnecessary risk while the IDF is operating under significant operational strain."

IDF criticises 'misuse' of resources, but not destruction of memorial

The damaged monument in the West Bank village of Madama bears the names of Palestinians killed in the war. (AP: Majdi Mohammed)

The military criticism appeared to focus on the diversion of resources, rather than the vandalism itself.

The IDF said it viewed the situation with the "utmost severity", and accused Mr Sukkot of "misuse of the protection provided by security forces".

"It should be emphasised that the IDF regularly dismantles symbols of incitement, subject to all required approvals and in coordination with the Civil Administration, as has occurred several times in recent months and and an additional operation is planned for the near future," it said.

"These activities are an important component of the fight against terrorism and incitement to terrorism."

Israel's Prime Minister also condemned the incident — from the perspective of the strain it put on the military.

"The IDF is the sovereign in Judea and Samaria and is responsible for implementing the decisions of the political echelon," Benjamin Netanyahu said in a statement.

"Taking the law into its own hands, especially by public figures, is wrong and prevents the IDF from focusing on its missions against terrorism and incitement."

Sukkot previously sanctioned for inciting violence against Palestinians

Zvi Sukkot is a member of the Religious Zionist party, led by right-wing finance minister Bezalel Smotrich — a man who has been sanctioned by the international community, including Australia, for inciting violence against Palestinians.

Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich leads the country's Religious Zionist Party. (Reuters: Ammar Awad)

Before entering politics, Mr Sukkot had been arrested on allegations of firebombing a mosque.

In 2024, he was among right-wing politicians who encouraged supporters to storm the notorious Sde Teiman detention facility in southern Israel after nine IDF reservists were arrested over the alleged brutal rape of a Palestinian detainee — an incident caught on CCTV, but later dropped by military prosecutors after immense political pressure.

Tensions in the area around Madama have been high in recent weeks, following a deadly shooting attack in the nearby village of Tell.

Two Israeli settlers and four Palestinians were killed in the incident — Israelis accusing the Palestinians of turning on them, while the Palestinians accused the settlers of being armed and aggressive.

The shooting prompted a large scale Israeli military operation in the area, detaining more than 100 Palestinians.

Israeli settlers in the area launched revenge attacks, destroying property and attacking residents.

Israeli media has reported the IDF having warned the Netanyahu government that the surge in settler violence has fuelled tensions in the West Bank, and it was effectively a tinderbox ready to blow.

World.title: Young Australians' home ownership rate at an 80-year low, report shows
World.content:
More young people are abandoning hopes of home ownership amid increasing generational inequality, according to a new report.

Anglicare's Falling Behind report, released on Tuesday, found home ownership among 25-34 year olds has fallen to an 80-year low — highlighting intergenerational inequality from tax settings that favoured housing investment.

Young Australians are facing a future where working hard does not guarantee security, Anglicare Australia executive director Kasy Chambers said after the report's release.

"The economic foundations underneath them have shifted," she said.

Ms Chambers said there was a perfect storm that led to inequality between the generations.

"What we can see is that we've got young people coming into a workforce that is more insecure, we can see that we've got increased costs," she said.

"People are studying longer. We know that it takes much longer to save a deposit for a house in terms of the annual average income versus the deposit."

Kasy Chambers has called for more measures to even the financial playing field. (AAP: Mick Tsikas)

Investment tax breaks fuelling the generational divide

Anglicare's report found older Australians "appear insulated" from today's economic pressures, having earned wages during a stable period in the job market and amassed wealth from investments which are taxed less severely than wages.

The report found that while older Australians' wealth has significantly increased over time, their share of income tax has not.

It said young people are "absorbing the impact" with lower wages proportional to house prices and cost of living — affording less opportunity to amass wealth.

The Albanese government this year introduced tax changes on investments including shares, investment properties and the sale of businesses.

What Labor's tax changes really mean for you Labor's capital gains tax changes have set off a firestorm of debate about the implications for small businesses, start-ups, share owners and plenty more. Here's who will really pay more.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers unveiled the sweeping changes in the May budget, describing them as the "most important and ambitious" reforms in decades, which would make the system "fairer and stronger for workers, businesses, first home buyers and future generations".

Ms Chambers welcomed the federal government's efforts to remove tax breaks for investment income, but said more measures were needed from the federal government to even the playing field.

"We need to look at taxing wealth the same way as income, because otherwise, what we're seeing is that the wealth gets concentrated," she told reporters in Canberra.

"Once it gets concentrated, it's very difficult to share that again ... one dollar is one dollar in taxation terms."

Low welfare payments prevent youth from catching up

Young Australians are eligible for less support from Centrelink despite facing the same costs as older people. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

The Anglicare head also called for a shake-up to the Youth Allowance payment, citing the report's findings that young Australians are eligible for less support from Centrelink despite facing the same costs as older people.

How will new unemployment changes affect Centrelink recipients? The federal government has proposed changes to Australia's $2 billion employment services system.

The maximum payment amount for a single person with no children on Youth Allowance is $677.20 a fortnight.

The rate is below the poverty line, JobSeeker and the aged pension, which Ms Chambers said is contributing to generational inequality.

"We have a social security system that literally says a young person needs less money to live on simply because of their age," Ms Chambers said.

"Rent isn't cheaper when you're 23. Groceries aren't cheaper. Electricity isn't cheaper. Yet young people are expected to survive on the lowest payment in the system.

" Poverty should not be a rite of passage. "

The report also highlighted that a single person on JobSeeker falls behind by $251 a week after paying for rent, food and transport — while a single parent on parenting payment falls behind by $174 a week and a couple with two children on JobSeeker falls behind by $428 a week.

It found nearly half of all low-income renters aged under 35 are experiencing rental stress, and not a single rental property across the country was affordable for a single person on the support payment.

World.title: Qantas doubles points, status ahead of credit card changes
World.content:
Travel newsAir travel Qantas doubles points, status ahead of credit card changes Chris Zappone August 26, 2026 — 12:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Qantas is dangling a fresh loyalty offer weeks before new rules are expected to put a dampener on consumers’ frequent flyer activity. From Wednesday until September 2, Qantas frequent flyers will be given double points, or double status credits, for any marketed flight. Qantas’ double points offer can also be applied to Qantas Hotel and Holiday bookings. Dedicated frequent flyers can also earn double status credits, which allow members to scale the frequent flyer tiers (bronze, silver, gold, platinum) faster, giving access to lounges and other perks. The offer comes just over a month before October 1 regulations by the Reserve Bank kick in. Already, the rules are prompting banks to offer fewer points on credit card sign-ups or on spending. (Banks typically purchase the points from airlines, funded in part by transaction fees which the RBA is eliminating).



Some Qantas frequent flyers wait for these specials, which happen once or twice a year, and make multiple bookings, allowing them to lock in their status credits (300 for silver, 700 for gold). The double points can also be applied to Qantas Hotel and Holiday bookings, providing an extra boost for those planning their next getaway, the airline said. 



Eliseo said it’s possible Qantas will reveal the start date for the change at the full-year results. Related Article Opinion

Travel tips What most people don’t understand about frequent flyer bookings Chris Chamberlin Million-mile flyer RBA changes are expected to alter the loyalty industry playing field further, spurring more activity at the retail level. Last week, CommBank unveiled its Yello rewards scheme, where points are earned from every-day spend and redeemed across a range of products, like shopping, gift cards and points transfers to airlines. CommBank’s partner is Virgin’s Velocity program. David Parsons, the chief executive of customer loyalty program consultancy Ellipsis, described the loyalty devaluations triggered by the RBA as “the biggest modern reset” of credit card and airline loyalty schemes. Parsons envisions a split in the market with smaller merchants retaining savings from not paying merchants fees, while Woolworths’ and Coles’ retail programs “keep investing and absorb the attention and spend that will depart from credit card loyalty”.



At the same time, “the airlines lose the daily reinforcement of a co-branded card tap”. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Batman socks, a dog fountain, a cafe corner: Quiet tributes for two fallen officers
World.content:
The police officers who went to Dezi Freeman’s remote home in Victoria’s high country to serve a warrant a year ago today say they didn’t know what they were walking into. But they knew they had two of their best officers with them. Veteran detective Neal Thompson was on his last proper job just days away from retiring while rising star, 35-year-old Vadim de Waart-Hottart, had recently arrived from Melbourne’s Public Order Response Squad. Neal Thompson (left) with his beloved dog Jimmy who passed away only months before the shootings, and Vadim de Waart-Hottart with the painting done for him by someone he helped on the job. In the ambush that followed, Freeman shot both officers dead, and injured another, before disappearing into the wilds of Mount Buffalo in Porepunkah. The murders sparked Australia’s biggest-ever manhunt, ending in Freeman’s death in a shootout seven months later and more than 100 kilometres away at the New South Wales border, and left a community – and two police families – devastated. On Tuesday, hundreds gathered outside the pair’s station in Wangaratta as police unveiled two memorials for Thompson and de Waart-Hottart, hewn from rock side by side. A dog fountain is coming too, for Thompson the dog-lover. And another plaque will be unveiled, further up the mountain in Bright, a year on from the killings on Wednesday.



Police Chief Commissioner Mike Bush said it would be “a solemn day for every single member of Victoria Police”. Ten officers went to Freeman’s off-grid property that day to “hold an alleged paedophile to account” as part of a child sexual abuse investigation, Bush said. “Over the last 12 months I have witnessed our organisation unite in times of utter shock and grief, all while remaining steadfast in finding answers for our beloved colleagues.” Mike Bush at the service at Wangaratta police station on Tuesday to unveil memorials for Neal Thompson and Vadim de Waart-Hottart. Joe Armao Many of those answers are still to emerge, ahead of inquests into both the August 26 shootings and Freeman’s final shootout with police when he refused to surrender in his shipping container hide-out near the border. The hunt is still on too for those who helped him on the run, after all those long months of searching and hundreds of police raids across the high country. But this week is not about Freeman, the sovereign citizen lionised by conspiracy theorists online. Nearby towns are heaving with loved ones of de Waart-Hottart and Thompson travelling up for the memorials.



Both men – two toweringly tall cops known for their love of adventure and compassion on the job – were adored not just by friends, but by former partners, as family. WhatsApp groups of ex-girlfriends, united by the tragedies, have been pinging with old photos and favourite memories. In one photo, Vadim holds a painting created for him by someone he helped on the job through a mental health crisis; tall Vadim in a swirl of chaos, listening with his hands clasped. A cloth Batman badge with the Belgium flag designed to honour Vadim de Waart-Hottart by his colleagues. Since his death, some of his former squad mates have taken to wearing a uniform not strictly police-issue: Batman socks and badges. De Waart-Hottart once joked he’d get thrown out of the police academy for wearing Batman socks, but he loved the caped crusader. His little brother Sacha, back home in Belgium where they’d grown up, had always said Vadim was his hero, his Batman, protecting him and now Vadim was out protecting his community. De Waart-Hottart did it all with a smile, acting commander Peta Barrett said Tuesday. In fact, he could never quite believe his own luck. He was brimming with tales of unexpected opportunities, she said, travel disasters that turned into kind offers of hospitality. His family sometimes joked that whenever they encountered their own good luck, they were “doing a Vadim”.



Last August, Vadim, the gentle giant who leapt out of aeroplanes, skied mountaintops and dived in the deep sea, had been excited to explore the Alpine wilderness on his new secondment in Porepunkah. At Thommo’s favourite cafe, run by close friend Anita Cook, a plaque by the bench on the left now reads “Neal’s corner” for his favourite spot where “he could see all the action”, Cook says. Jason South In a cafe just down the road from Wangaratta in Moyhu, a nondescript gold plaque by the bench on the left now reads “Neal’s corner”. This was Thompson’s favourite cafe, run by his close friend Anita Cook. Most mornings, Thompson, or “Thommo” as he was known around town, would slip in early, by the side door, for eggs on the way through from his farm to work, his wire-haired pointer Jimmy at his heels. “He’d always sneak in to surprise me,” says Cook. “He’d have my staff here all intimidated, you know ‘the detective’s in’, but he’d have that smirk. He was a big softie and if you were in, in his circle of trust, he’d do anything for you.” His sisters Dianne Thompson and Lois Kirk, who joined de Waart-Hottart’s aunt at the Wangaratta memorial on Tuesday, said their big brother had followed their grandfather into the police force, and “truly loved his job”. He was “fiercely loyal, a natural leader”, as tough as he was soft.



Thompson’s girlfriend Sergeant Lisa Thompson said every day since losing him had felt surreal. “Nothing will fill the hole Neal’s loss leaves behind, but his stoic words, ‘C’mon, get on with it!’, and the lessons he shared with us, give [us] the strength to keep going,” she said. Thompson was an experienced bushman, who knew the beautiful but treacherous terrain of the wet Alpine valley well. While he was going to miss the job in retirement, he had grand adventures planned too, alongside his best friends Andrew “Crouchy” Crouch and Dirk Wendt. He had some Steve Irwin in him, Wendt says, or perhaps it was the accident-prone Russell Coight – known for his fascination with wildlife and fast MacGyver fixes (including the more-than-occasional stuff up) out in the bush. Thompson’s best friend Dirk Wendt brings his own dog Beau, brother of Thompson’s beloved late dog Jimmy, and Jimmy’s daughter dog Ivy, to visit the new memorial. Joe Armao Thompson’s ex-partner and friend Ange Creighton recalls with fondness the disaster of one of their early dates, a camping trip, when Thommo nearly sank the boat. “Then he wanted me to go rock climbing with him and I thought hmm, maybe not.



As a surprise for Thompson’s upcoming retirement, his station had made special beer stubbies: Thommo immortalised as ‘The Don’ from The Godfather. “But he had this incredible focus with it, like he had with gun safety and especially with his work, too, for all the silly stuff he did out of hours.” Thompson knew Freeman, and had gone along that day to help keep him calm. “He’d have been so careful,” says Creighton. “He was great at building rapport. Quite a few of the local crooks were sad when he died.” His favourite crook even had a nickname for Thommo: “The Don”. As a surprise for his last shift the week of the shooting, Thompson’s police station had made special beer stubbies: Thommo immortalised as ‘The Don’ from The Godfather, with the slicked back hair and a better suit than he’d ever worn himself.



Related Article Good Weekend ‘Thommo’ was days from retirement when he walked into an ambush. Today, his colleagues remember him “As soon as I heard about the shooting, I knew it’d be him,” says Cook, who had served Thommo as usual on his way through her cafe before work that morning. “He was always, you know, send junior to the back, ‘I’ll go in first’.” ”He was, kind of, the man that I’d call on, if I needed anything. Even when he died, he had my steel on the back of his car to take to the wreckers for me. So to not have that ... because you know I’m just on my own.” Bush said that Victoria Police will now “carry forth Neal and Vadim’s legacies for the rest of time”. De Waart-Hottart’s mother Carolina and father Alain said the love for Vadim in his new home of Victoria had brought them immense comfort, including in Porepunkah – a place named for an Aboriginal word meaning the meeting of two rivers.



“Here, at this meeting place, we honour both rivers,” they said in a tribute published in full below. “The river of grief for the life we have lost, and the river of love for the life Vadim gave us.” With John Silvester The Two Rivers Grief is a river that now runs through all our lives, unmapped, shoreless, the nature of mourning. The death of Vadim, our son, Sacha’s brother and your brother in this noble family of blue has brought us together today. For there are now two rivers flowing in our lives connecting us forever.The river of loss and grief and the river of life and love.This river of life is always flowing forwards to join with the vastness of the eternal ocean. So too are we all destined to return to the eternal. No energy is ever lost; it is simply transformed. Death is the only promise held. The transient moving towards the eternalWe have the capacity to hold both emotions:Grief and joy.Sorrow and gratitude.Sadness and happiness.Absence and presence.While we are grieving the trauma of a young life that was taken from us, we simultaneously hold in our hearts our happy memories of his life lived with passion, enthusiasm, generosity and pure love of life with his trademark ever present infectious smile. We also feel gratitude for the life we still have the grace to live now. Grief is not something we can simply choose to leave behind. It is a powerful and overwhelming emotion, and we need to find the grace to flow with it; to allow ourselves to be carried by its current when we need to. But there are moments when we can choose which river we wish to turn towards: the river of grief, which can drag us down into the muddy depths of sorrow; or the river of life, where we can consciously harness the winds and fill our sails with all that is joyous. We cannot stop the river of grief from flowing through us. But we can learn to flow with it, and, when we are ready, to lift our eyes towards the river of life and allow ourselves to be carried forward. When two rivers meet, they merge, blending their distinct waters, each carrying different stories. There are times when the rivers join, as we experience both emotions of grief and love simultaneously. There are times the rivers will part travelling over new terrains.Just like a confluence where two rivers collide, the initial meeting of deep grief is turbulent and churning before it finds a broader, steadier flow. The river does not become wider by forcing one current to disappear. It becomes wider allowing both currents to coexist.As we too must embrace the grief and the love.For I have learnt to see that grief is the mirror of love.We are living in two realities: the physical and the cosmic.It is said that this grief is love with nowhere to go.So let us all give it somewhere to go, let it sense gratitude for what we have. Let the river teach us that we can hold both stillness and storm, flexibility and strength, become a rapid or a quiet reflecting pool.Let the stars remind us that light is revealed in the darkness.To have known the light that is Vadim has brought us all much laughter and kindness. We all now walk the banks of the river of life hand in hand. Our family feel a deep connection and gratitude to all of you here today, one year after Vadim’s departure. We are especially grateful to those who were with Vadim in his final moments on earth, at Porpunkah, the aboriginal word for the ‘meeting of two rivers’. Here, at this meeting place, we honour both rivers: the river of grief for the life we have lost, and the river of love for the life Vadim gave us. And so, as we continue along the river of life, we carry Vadim with us — in our memories, in our love, and in the light he left behind. Two rivers, meeting in one place, flowing together towards the eternal. -De Waart-Hottart family Be the first to know when major news happens.
