World.title: Beijing warns it will not sever ties with Iran after US vows ‘economic D-Day’
World.content:
WorldAsiaTrade wars Beijing warns it will not sever ties with Iran after US vows ‘economic D-Day’ Lisa Visentin August 25, 2026 — 10:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Beijing: China has fired a warning shot at Washington, making clear it won’t cease cooperating with Iran and was prepared to retaliate if the Trump administration continued with fresh sanctions. In a move that sets up another potential collision course with Beijing, US Treasury Scott Bessent this week declared an “economic D-Day” on Iran, seeking to sever its remaining financial lifelines by hitting collaborators with sanctions. Beijing responded on Tuesday by defending its ties with Tehran, and warning it would not bow down to US pressure. Donald Trump and Xi Jinping are expected to meet for a high-stakes summit at the White House next month. Getty “China’s cooperation with Iran has always been conducted within the international framework and should not be interfered with or undermined,” Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Lin Jian said at a press conference in Beijing.



Related Article Analysis

Middle East at war The White House says this is the Iran endgame. We’ve heard that before “China is closely monitoring relevant developments and will take all necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own interests.” China buys as much as 90 per cent of Iran’s oil, providing Tehran with a critical source of revenue that helps sustain the Islamic regime in the face of crippling sanctions. Any move by the US to truly strangle Iran’s finances would have to take aim at its trade ties with China, and in particular, the Chinese banks processing oil payment transactions. Such an escalation would almost certainly blow up the fragile trade truce struck between US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping last year, and derail the leaders’ high-stakes summit at the White House next month, something both Beijing and Washington have otherwise appeared intent on avoiding.



The Trump administration has given few details about exactly how it will economically decapitate Iran, other than broadly threaten foreign entities with exclusion from the US financial system if they continued to do business with Tehran. Related Article Updated

Middle East at war US launches ‘Operation Economic Outcast’ to isolate Iran from the world While declaring that no country would be exempt, Bessent made clear the US was not prepared to go after the Chinese banks. “We are giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behaviour. Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” he said on Monday (US time). Meanwhile, the US Treasury Department unveiled a package of fresh sanctions against 60 entities, including logistics and shipping companies based in Hong Kong and mainland China, but it avoided targeting major Chinese financial institutions.



China has condemned the sanctions as unilateral measures that will only worsen conflicts and called for a return to negotiations. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Gawn makes All-Australian history, but Dawson’s moving speech steals the show
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Gawn makes All-Australian history, but Dawson’s moving speech steals the show Jon Pierik August 25, 2026 — 9:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Melbourne captain Max Gawn has capped a record ninth All-Australian selection by being named captain, but the biggest moment of the night came when his Adelaide counterpart Jordan Dawson was named to the side for the third time. On the field, the Crows skipper had a year to remember, but off-field he endured unimaginable heartbreak with the loss of his elder brother, Jaryd. Jonathan Brown interviews Max Gawn in one of the moments of the night at Centrepiece at Melbourne Park. AFL Photos In paying tribute to Dawson, Gawn said he knew who showed the most leadership this season – the No.12 for Adelaide. “I think we saw leadership tonight,” Gawn said.



“For Jordan to get up and do what he did, to lead his side … to show vulnerability in front of a group of strangers … that’s a captain that I want to be behind.” Earlier, Dawson – this year’s All-Australian vice captain – gave a spine-tingling speech about the importance of speaking up when times are tough. View post on X “I just want to wish anyone who’s struggled with mental health out there, or who is struggling with mental health, to know you are loved, and the world is a better place with you in it” On the football front, there were several controversial omissions in the 23-man team unveiled on Tuesday night.



Gawn became the first man to earn nine green blazers and was honoured to also assume the captaincy, a role Demons coach Steven King last week said he deserved. Gawn had captained the All-Australian side once before, in 2021. Record breaker: Melbourne captain Max Gawn has received his ninth All-Australian blazer. AFL Photos Western Bulldogs counterpart Marcus Bontempelli joined a select group of eight – Gary Ablett snr, Gary Ablett jnr, Patrick Dangerfield, Lance Franklin, Robert Harvey and Mark Ricciuto – to have enjoyed the top honour eight times. A record five Indigenous players were named – Wayne Milera, Jarman Impey, Kysaiah Pickett, Shai Bolton and Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera. The record had been four players in 2006, when Shaun Burgoyne, Lindsay Gilbee, Adam Goodes and Andrew McLeod were honoured. Loading



The club-imposed suspension of Sydney players Nick Blakey, Isaac Heeney and Chad Warner – almost certainly all would have been selected – opened up three spots, but there were still contentious selections. Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 Butters declares he’s leaving Port, but he won’t get to Collingwood. Suns spearhead also on the move Zak Butters, despite playing only 17 games because of injury, was chosen ahead of Hawthorn co-captain Jai Newcombe, and Carlton superstar Patrick Cripps, who has been integral to the Blues’ rise under Josh Fraser. Port Adelaide defender Aliir Aliir was also a surprise omission, while teammate Jason Horne-Francis also had strong claims. Geelong wingman Oliver Dempsey was one of nine maiden All-Australians, the young star redefining how his role is played through his ability to push forward and kick goals. However, Dempsey was chosen ahead of star teammate Max Holmes, who was in superb touch, averaging 29 disposals, before a right ankle fracture and syndesmosis injury in July.



Emerging Fremantle gun Murphy Reid donned a blazer in just his second year in the AFL, an outstanding achievement. All told, 10 players retained their spots from the 2025 team – Gawn, Bontempelli, Dawson, Wanganeen-Milera, Pickett, Jordan Clark, Harris Andrews, Bailey Smith, Zac Bailey and Nick Daicos. The full list of club representation was: Adelaide (two), Brisbane Lions (three), Collingwood (one), Fremantle (five), Geelong (two), GWS (one), Hawthorn (two), Melbourne (two), Port Adelaide (one), St Kilda (two), Sydney Swans (one) and Western Bulldogs (one). The selection panel included AFL CEO Andrew Dillon (chair), Eddie Betts, Simon Black, Jude Bolton, Abbey Holmes, Glen Jakovich, Laura Kane, David Mundy, Joel Selwood and Greg Swann.



Meanwhile, Daicos, now a three-time All Australian, was crowned the AFL Players’ Association most valuable player for a second time, capping a fine season in which he polled 147 votes – a new benchmark. Daicos, having averaged a whopping 35 disposals per game, beat Bontempelli (109 votes) and Gawn (99) to the honour. He also won the award in 2024. He surpassed Richmond champion Dustin Martin’s previous benchmark of 122 votes in 2017. “We are incredibly proud of what he has achieved and even more so for the way he approaches his game in all phases. On-field and off-field, Nick sets the standard at our club and is a wonderful leader. We want our program not just to develop great players, but incredible people and Nick really represents that,” Magpies coach Craig McRae said. St Kilda co-captain Callum Wilkie claimed the inaugural AFL Coaches Association defensive player of the year. Wilkie finished the home-and-away season with 42 votes, ahead of Brisbane’s Andrews, Sydney’s Tom McCartin and Geelong’s Connor O’Sullivan, who each polled 30 votes.



Dockers star Reid and St Kilda’s Max Hall shared the AFLCA’s best emerging player award. Support is available from Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Government looks to tighten up wholesale investment rules
World.content:
The government is looking to tighten up the rules covering wholesale investment offers, amid concern the current rules are too permissive.

A report by law firm Chapman Tripp says proposed reforms set out in a Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) discussion document could attract "significant industry pushback" particularly on the promotion of wholesale investment offers.

The changes contemplated by MBIE focus on whether:

The eligible investor test is too permissive

The two-year renewal cycle for investor certification is too short

The promotion of wholesale offers to the general public should be more tightly constrained

The various thresholds for wholesale investor status should be adjusted.

Chapman Tripp partner Penny Sheerin said wholesale investment offers were not suitable for inexperienced investors.

"The risk to people offering these deals at the moment is that they have investors who are unsuitable within their investor base, who are really retail investors, who are perhaps inappropriately certifying themselves as eligible investors because they wish to participate in a wholesale offer that may appear attractive to them, but isn't actually suitable for them based on their level of experience in investing," Sheerin said.

The Chapman Tripp report also warned there were risks the regulations could go too far.

"So, for example, I think going too far would be licensing wholesale offerors," Sheerin said.

"That would be something that we wouldn't support, particularly given the global portability of capital and the risk that New Zealand investors may just then simply invest offshore."

The report said some of the reforms could add unnecessary compliance costs.

The partners said concerns about inappropriate advertising of wholesale offers were legitimate, but it was critical that the detailed implementation did not unduly restrict capital-raising in the wholesale sector.

"We are not aware of other countries seeking to licence wholesale offerors and would not support such a move given the global portability of capital and the risk that New Zealand investors may simply invest offshore," the report said, adding there were better ways to manage the risks.

The report said wholesale offers were already under the microscope through the Financial Market Authority's (FMA) recent regulatory proceedings and enforcement actions, with an ongoing focus on wholesale issuer conduct, a thematic review in late 2022, and the High Court judgement concerning eligible investor certificates in late 2025.

World.title: West Coast in for a lashing of heavy rain over the next three days
World.content:
MetService says the South Island will bear the brunt of a complex low pressure system which will bring heavy rain to the West Coast over the next three days, from midday Wednesday.

A cold snap was forecast to bring heavy snow to the Canterbury High Country south of the Rangitata River and north of the stretch between Arrowtown and Ranfurly from 6pm, carrying on through until Friday morning.

Rain over the Crown Range Road was also expected to turn to snow on high parts of the road later Wednesday morning.

MetService meteorologist Braydon White said farmers on the eastern side of the divide of the central South Island - including Mount Cook and potentially Twizel - should prepare livestock for a sudden shift from previously warm conditions to a significant amount of snow above 800 metres with lesser amounts forecast to fall as low as 400 metres.

"Going into a much colder situation in the next couple of days, you'll want to make sure that your livestock are doing okay, making sure you have plans in place if you've got any young lambs starting to appear," White said.

He said motorists in the area should consider changing their routes to avoid the higher passes and ensure they had snow chains, sleeping bags, warm clothing, and emergency items with them.

"If you do have to travel, maybe consider having a go bag in your car, just in case you get trapped," White said.

A swollen Twizel River in September 2023. RNZ / Nathan McKinnon

Meanwhile, on the western side of the island, a low pressure system - which was travelling down from the east coast of Australia - could see up to 500mm of rain about the Westland ranges with nearly 200mm expected to fall nearer the coast.

The rain was expected to peak at three points across the coming days - reaching up to 30 mm/h on Wednesday afternoon and evening, then again on Thursday evening and in a final burst on Friday morning.

"This fairly complex system is quite wavy and so what happens is you get one wave pushing into the Alps, dumping a whole lot of rain and then it'll ease off for a bit of time as the next wave approaches from the sea.

"So part of the reason this is such an extended period is because we're capturing two or three waves as they all funnel through," White said.

White said the drawn-out nature of the rainfall could make the rain across the area a little less severe than the numbers might initially suggest.

"Because it's not all falling in a very short amount of time, that gives time for the rivers to really just get the water away. So while it is quite a bit of rain, if there was anywhere in the country that was going to handle that reasonably well, it would be Westland.

"Certainly there's risk of rivers rising rapidly or slips and potentially road disruption for a time of flooding that could cut places off. But it's hard to be more certain about just how bad it could get," White said.

Mist and clouds hover over the area near the road to Franz Josef glacier on 19 January, 2024. RNZ / Tess Brunton

Heavy rain watches were also in place for Grey and Buller south of Westport, the headwaters of the Canterbury lakes and rivers about and south of Arthur's Pass, Otago headwaters and Fiordland north of Caswell Sound, White said.

"So while we're expecting the focus of that rain to be the Westland area, the waviness of the system does mean that it moves north and south at times, and so certainly outside of that Westland area we'll still see some decent bursts of heavy rain.

"Alongside that, the north-westerly system will be a bit stronger and that will allow that rain to push over the Alps and into the Canterbury and Otago headwaters as well," White said.

World.title: Storing carbon in sea could have huge potential for fighting climate change - report
World.content:
Storing carbon in the sea could have huge potential for fighting climate change but will need careful oversight because of its risks, a new report says.

A Royal Society of New Zealand report, released on Wednesday, said even a drastic reduction in emissions was no longer enough to keep global temperatures within the 1.5°C warming limit set out in the Paris Agreement.

Directly removing carbon dioxide already in the atmosphere would also be necessar.

New Zealand already removes millions of tonnes of CO2 each year through forestry, but technology to also store the gas in the sea was emerging, the report said.

"Marine carbon dioxide removal may be a future tool to help reduce atmospheric carbon levels."

Marine carbon dioxide removal, or mCDR, ranged from restoring and maintaining 'blue carbon' environments like mangroves, wetlands and salt marshes, to deliberately altering the chemistry of the ocean to allow it to absorb more CO2.

Read more about marine carbon dioxide removal in this RNZ explainer, published earlier in 2026.

Almost all of the techniques were at an early stage, the report said.

"Currently, mCDR is a collection of developing technologies that are not yet ready for large-scale deployment."

There was "significant uncertainty" about how well each technique worked, whether they could be scaled, how long carbon would be locked away for, the costs, and the environmental risks and side effects.

"Any potential mCDR technique would require more research, effective monitoring and verification, and in-depth societal discussions before considering large-scale use," it said.

Despite growing interest, there was "minimal regulation" for marine carbon dioxide removal in New Zealand.

At the moment, New Zealand's exclusive economic zone regulations, together with international laws governing the ocean, control what can be done in the country's waters.

They prohibit marine dumping and 'placement of matter', although there is an exclusion for legitimate scientific research.

New Zealand's regulations were developed before marine geengineering and mDCR technologies emerged.

At least one mCDR company, Gigablue, has been pushing for changes to allow it to carry out larger-scale research and future commercial activitites.

Restoring or maintaining mangroves is a 'blue carbon' technology that is already in use - but the report warns that habitats that degrade or are damaged in storms could release their stored carbon again. Veronika Meduna / RNZ

The Royal Society report said mCDR presented potential economic opportunities for coastal communities, but also risks, "if projects fail or damage the marine environment".

Ahead of any adoption, "New Zealand, together with our Pacific neighbours, will need to establish appropriate regulations and governance," it said.

Victoria University earth sciences professor Tim Naish, a veteran climate researcher, said some carbon removals on land or sea would be necessary to reverse climate warming.

However, they risked creating a "moral hazard" by allowing societies to keep emitting.

"We create this idea that we don't really need to reduce emissions - we can do other things," he said.

"If you create a narrative that, oh, she'll be right, we can get out of this with technology and clever use of natural sinks - I do worry about that."

Carbon removals would have to continue as long as humans kept creating emissions, rather than cutting them at their source.

"It's not just one dump of alkaline basalt in the ocean... It's got to be continuously done."

That could be both financially and environmentally costly, Naish said.

It was worth considering whether New Zealand could put its large amount of ocean to use, but there was plenty the country should be doing first.

"We're not even doing our bit on emissions reduction," he said.

World.title: Public raise almost $30k in support of injured Palmerston North police officer
World.content:
The organiser of a Givealittle page in support of a Palmerston North police officer critically injured over the weekend says the community's response has been "remarkable".

The officer was deploying road spikes ahead of a fleeing vehicle on Kairanga Bunnythorpe Road about 2am on Saturday, when he was struck and thrown several metres.

He was airlifted to Wellington Hospital in a critical condition, while a second officer was treated for minor injuries.

Police filed charges against two teenage boys in relation to the incident.

The scene where the officer was injured. RNZ/Jimmy Ellingham

Givealittle page organiser Dame Therese Walsh said she understood the officer was only "a couple of years out of police college" and had a young family.

She'd reached out to the officer's family and - while they were reluctant to be in the public eye - they agreed to allow her to set up the page.

"It's not a step they wanted to take lightly. But of course, with a young family and with a lot of unintended expenses that come out of a situation like this. I think they were keen for some support.

"The New Zealand Police are very good to their injured officers as well, but you know that the expenses do pile up when you're in a situation like this and the future is a little unknown," Walsh said.

Walsh said the page was well on track to reach $30,000 worth of donations by the end of its second day online on Tuesday.

Dame Therese Walsh. (File photo) RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

At the time of writing donations were already in excess of $29,000.

"I just feel a sense of community coming through with this. I think in a really volatile world to have moments where people come together with that strong sense of community to help somebody who's going to work every day to help all of us is quite special.

"As I've seen this Givealittle page grow, I have felt that deep sense of humanity and you know that's a wonderful thing," Walsh said.

Walsh said - as a patron for a police recruitment wing in 2023 - she was immediately concerned when she heard news of the officer's injuries.

"I did a number of training sessions with them and got to know them well. So whenever I hear something about the police, I always take notice to see if it's one of the recruits from that time. It wasn't, but I still have a great deal of empathy for what people in the police go through on the front line.

"And sitting through some of those training sessions, they deal with some really tough stuff. So it just really got me thinking and I wanted to do something to help."

Walsh said the family had asked her to pass on their gratitude for the thought, prayers and donations from the public.

"At this difficult time they were just wanting to focus on being at his bedside," she said.

Walsh said she understood the officer remained in a coma in Wellington Hospital.

On Sunday Central District Commander Superintendent Dion Bennett said the officer was in a stable condition and remained on a ventilator in hospital.

World.title: Woolworths Sunnynook closed after pedestrian hit by vehicle in carpark
World.content:
A supermarket on Auckland's North Shore is closed until further notice after a crash in the store's car park.

Police said the crash, which involved a pedestrian, was reported at 6.30pm on Tuesday, and initial reports indicated there were serious injuries.

Woolworths Sunnynook said it was co-operating with emergency services at the scene.

World.title: National MPs 'misappropriate' time for questions in the House
World.content:
National is being accused of making a mockery of Parliament's processes by deliberately not giving itself enough time to answer questions from Opposition MPs in the House.

Leader of the House Louise Upston says National has tried to fix the system to ensure that does not happen, but not all parties agreed on proposed changes.

In the House on Tuesday, MPs took part in the Estimates debate, which scrutinises Budget spending decisions.

The debate runs for 11 hours over a number of sitting days.

Each party is given a certain amount of time to speak, spread across the course of the debate, and the party whips allocate that time between their members.

Nearing the end of the debate on Tuesday afternoon, Upston - in her capacity as Social Development Minister - refused to continue answering questions because her time allocation was up.

Chair Greg O'Connor had earlier warned members asking questions to be mindful of that.

"Her colleagues before have... let's just say, misappropriated her time," he said.

Upston answered some further questions from the Greens' Ricardo Menéndez March and Labour's Willow-Jean Prime, then stopped.

"I have no more time, I'm not speaking, all right, so I don't want to upset anyone, we've tried to improve this process and the Labour Party didn't agree," she said.

"You're speaking right now!" Menéndez March said.

O'Connor said MPs could continue to ask questions, but it was up to National how it allocated its time.

Questions continued, but Upston did not.

"Mr Chair, we have an allocation, I'm not going to take time off following ministers where there are energy, resources, health and housing (still to be debated)," said Upston.

Menéndez March asked to grant 15 seconds of his own allocated time to Upston so she could give yes or no answers, which O'Connor allowed.

"Doesn't mean I'm gonna use it," Upston said.

She answered one further question, then stayed silent.

"Crickets," Prime said.

Menéndez March later told RNZ ministers were entitled to do that, but it showed National did not take scrutiny of the executive seriously, choosing to give lengthy speeches in answer to simple questions to run down the clock.

"It makes a mockery of a process that is supposed to allow for the scrutiny of ministers, and for ministers to be accountable to decisions that they have made," he said.

"It is up to the National Party on how to manage that time, but when throughout the debate you see ministers using their time to give political speeches and throw platitudes instead of answering questions, it is no surprise that as we draw close to the end of this debate, ministers are choosing to not answer questions."

Menéndez March said he did not get adequate answers to questions about whether any beneficiaries lost payments as part of a new policy change, and about cuts to the accommodation supplement for low-income homeowners.

Upston said National had proposed trialling a change to the Estimates debate to ensure ministers would not run out of time.

"National has sought to make improvements to what we know is not a great system but these haven't been agreed to by all parties," she said.

"We agree the format doesn't work as it should."

World.title: Youths on proposed social media ban: Cautious approval, but questions around enforcement
World.content:
Young people question proposed social media ban Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

"How are you going to enforce this?" That's the response from young people who grew up with social media to the proposed ban for under-16s.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said social media is exposing young people to harmful content, addictive technology and pressure they aren't equipped to deal with, and the government would push ahead with the Online Safety Bill.

"We would never knowingly let our children wander into places in the real world we know to be unsafe. We put boundaries around cars, around alcohol, around gambling, because we know children aren't yet equipped for them."

So, it has been proposed that social media platforms will risk financial penalties if they don't take steps to verify the age of users.

But some Auckland 17- and 18-year-olds say they're not convinced a complete ban will work.

For some teens who jumped on to social media around 12 years old, some of what the government mentioned during their announcement resembled their experiences.

Checkpoint spoke with some Year 13 students from Auckland's Albany Senior High School.

Jeremy Ouwejan said he often saw content that came from online communities such as the manosphere.

"Andrew Tate speaking to young impressionable men about very damaging ideologies like misogyny, transphobia and homophobia, or, armchair psychology that says how to manipulate your friends and how to do certain things.

Andrew Tate. AFP / DANIEL MIHAILESCU

"Or people will say, 'I used to be a dietitian, here's what you should and shouldn't eat.' [Instagram] Reels on working out and harmful gym content saying, 'If you're not benching 100kg are you even a real person?'"

Ouwejan said he also had seen posts that were violent.

"I'll hop onto Reels and I'll be flashed with a [dead] body. It'll completely ruin the experience of just wanting to talk to a friend."

Last year, research from Te Mana Whakaatu / The Classification Office, found young people don't generally go looking for objectionable content. But it could be hard to avoid when it came up on social media, in group chats or was shown around in person.

Some examples of this included pornography and real-world violence.

Another student, Natalie Osmond, told Checkpoint coming across extreme, violent and misogynistic content every day took a toll.

"When you're giving people ranked numerical scores, especially women… it's objectification to the highest level. You can't just put a number value on someone, it's bad it comes with the podcasts.

"A lot of my feed is about Ariana Grande for example, and other female artists. The [comments] will be all about body image and they're just saying horrible things."

Ariana Grande. CHRIS DELMAS

But, she said, social media also came with its positives.

"Social media is also a good way to get informed from people. There's a fine line between getting informed and seeing all of the bad stuff.

"I do think it's a crazy time to be alive and we can see what's going on in any corner of the world."

Osmond agreed restricting some parts of social media and having consequences for creating or promoting harmful content was a good thing.

"I wish it was socially acceptable to have a Nokia brick - I know I could actually do that, but I really couldn't.

"Also, even as a child I remember being 12 years old and it would socially stunt you even if you weren't allowed social media... you're pressured to have it from a very young age."

But Osmond and the other students Checkpoint spoke to weren't convinced a ban would work, with reports from Australia of teens using loopholes to get around it.

Ouwejan said change was needed, but had to be thought through.

"I think currently there is a lot of very young people on some very damaging platforms, and it is changing them for the worse for the rest of their lives.

"However, as we have seen from Australia and what we can interpolate from other studies and other bans, banning is not the way to go - we need a controlled method, but balancing that with free speech."

Another student, Isabella Green, said she was concerned around how the government would enforce a ban.

"How are you going to track and enforce this? That doesn't feel like it's something that would respect the privacy of people."

ACT and New Zealand First will not support the bill, meaning National will need Labour's support if it's to progress.

Not enough evidence - commissioner

Doubts over whether social media ban is enforceable Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

Children's Commissioner Jane Searle told Checkpoint more evidence into the effectiveness of a complete ban was needed before implementing one in Aotearoa.

"We know that [kids have told] us that they want the internet to be made safer or online harm to be reduced for them. Whether the solution is just in a complete ban, that remains to be seen, and we need to look at the evidence around that."

Children's Commissioner Jane Searle. Stephen Barker / Barker Photography via Child Matters

Searle said that a more comprehensive plan to tackle the issues around social media was needed, rather than just an outright ban.

"I think that we need good education for young people and their families to be able to make good decisions that keep them safe. But we also need to be able to hold tech companies to account and have robust obligations on them.

"Then we need to look at the regulation - do we have an independent regulator?"

She said there was also a concern over young people who may be marginalised or isolated as the result of a ban.

"We need to be very careful when we move forward, and we need to look at the evidence. We need to know, what will this ban look like in practice? How will it actually impact the way that young people are engaging with social media?"

Searle said there wasn't currently enough information to know if a ban would be successful.

"Even if you look at other countries, what they've implemented, it wasn't long ago, so we don't have that evidence to know."

She said more onus needed to be put on social media companies to manage what content they were showing to young people.

"It's about how they design the algorithms, how they engage with young people, how they put checks in places on what age and what is age appropriate."

However, she acknowledged that enforcing regulations on large tech companies would be difficult.

"I think we need to try and we need to put as much in place as possible. And then hopefully we can work with other governments around the world to actually have some influence as well."

World.title: Man found guilty of threatening to kill people at two Auckland schools
World.content:
A man has been found guilty of threatening to kill people at two Auckland schools and saying he would destroy police stations and buildings at Parliament.

A jury in the Manukau District Court today found Tiedan Huo guilty of 12 charges relating to threats against Waiuku and Rutherford colleges and other public buildings.

Huo was also convicted for unlawful possession of a firearm, unlawful possession of explosives and possession of objectionable material.

Huo denied all charges and mid-way through the trial elected to act for himself in place of the lawyers who had been acting for him.

The charges stemmed from a manifesto, in which he spoke of using 3D-printed firearms in an attack.

The jury took just under three hours to find him guilty on all charges.

In his opening address to the jury, Crown prosecutor Gareth Kayes said that on 12 March last year, staff at Waiuku College woke to a chilling email that had been sent at 1.42am.

"It was titled 'Important: Don't come to school tomorrow'. And it started with the words 'This is my manifesto'."

The email spoke of being bullied and humiliated by teachers at the school, being unfairly treated by police and being made to feel like a second-class citizen for being Chinese.

"I am going to do something about this now. I have began [sic] preparing for doing something about this since February this year and have finished now."

The email went on to set out in some detail the preparations the sender said they had made to carry out attacks on Waiuku and Rutherford colleges, as well as damaging the Pukekohe and Te Atatu police stations and buildings at Parliament.

That included making firearms using a 3D printer and creating bullets and explosives to be used in an attack.

The sender said they wanted to kill more people than the Christchurch mosque terrorist, who murdered 51 innocent people on 15 March 2019.

"Do not assume that my guns will not work or are fake because they are 3D printed, that will be very bad."

The email was purportedly sent by a female former Waiuku College student, but after she allowed police to examine her electronic devices, officers established this was not the case, and their inquiries led them to Huo.

World.title: Crows captain makes tearful speech as All Australian team is named
World.content:
Max Gawn has claimed a record ninth All Australian blazer, while Nick Daicos was named player of the year by both the coaches and his fellow players, but a speech from Adelaide captain Jordan Dawson stole the show at the AFL Awards.

Dawson won Best Captain and Most Courageous Player, before being selected in and named vice captain of the All Australian team, and spoke openly about his mental health on stage.

Dawson's brother died at the age of 35 earlier this year, something he says he has struggled to deal with throughout the season.

"It's been a struggle. It's not easy. It's a range of emotions and they come at different times," Dawson said.

"For me it's about creating safe spaces in the footy club and at home, and understanding there will be times when it's hard to go to work and that it is OK to feel a certain type of way.

"It's still raw, it's always going to be hard to talk about. I'm so lucky I have such supportive people around me.

"The mental health space is something new to me, but something I want to learn more about.

"I want everyone to know who is struggling with their mental health that you are definitely loved and that the world is a better place with you in it. You are enough. We all love you, you have friends and family around you."

Nick Daicos was a multiple winner at the AFL Awards. (Getty Images: Michael Willson)

Gawn, who was named captain of the All Australian side, became the first man to earn nine blazers. Marcus Bontempelli earned selection for an eighth time.

Daicos, selected in the All Australian time for the fourth time in the first five years of his career, also swept the Coaches Association Champion Player of the Year and Leigh Matthews MVP awards.

Carlton's Jagga Smith was named the Rising Star for 2026.

World.title: Richmond denies players 'making light' of Swans scandal on Mad Monday
World.content:
The Richmond Football Club has denied its players were "referencing or making light of recent matters" in footage recorded during their post-season celebrations.

Tiger players were recorded during a drinking session at a Victorian country pub, with one player seen feigning shock after being spanked on his rear by a teammate.

Another teammate whips a fellow player on the back with a belt in footage captured by news outlets yesterday, leading to speculation they were referencing the ongoing Sydney Swans scandal.

The club denied that was the case.

"Richmond is aware of a video circulating from a player end-of-season gathering," a statement read.

"The club has spoken to the players who have expressed their embarrassment over their behaviour.

"The players are adamant they were in no way referencing or making light of recent matters."

Swans will not be invited to Brownlow ceremony AFL boss Andrew Dillon speaks to the media about the Sydney Swans scandal, saying "the actions of a few don't define the actions of the entire industry".

The Tigers finished second last this season with a 3-20 win-loss record.

The pub that hosted Richmond's drinks said the controversy had been blown out of proportion.

"In our view, this has been blown out of proportion," the Garfield Hotel, 80 kilometres east of Melbourne, said in a statement posted on social media.

The hotel said it "could not speak more highly" of how players behaved.

"For such a young group, they were extremely respectful and a fun group of boys to deal with," the statement read.

Nick Blakey (left) is one of the Swans suspended for breaching club standards. (AAP Image: Dean Lewins)

"They enjoyed a few quiet beers to unwind after a long season and we see nothing wrong with that.

"They had booked out the venue for the afternoon, so they were the only patrons on site.

"They enjoyed their afternoon and moved on."

The hotel noted media were waiting for the Tigers players "in the hope of capturing a misstep, which we consider disappointing".

The Richmond footage emerged hours after AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon fronted the media for the first time since the Swans scandal began.

"I have been asked a lot in recent days, what message football should be sending young people and what we should be saying to our kids," Dillon said.

"For me, the answer is straightforward: it doesn't matter who you are, it doesn't matter what you do, whether you're an AFL footballer — the way we treat women says a lot about who we are as people, as a community and as a game.

"Quite simply, respect for women is not negotiable."

Dillon said the actions of the five suspended Swans players had "fallen well short of the standards our game expects and community deserves".

"While there are players involved, we cannot lose sight of the bigger picture. More importantly, there are women who have made a report to police and they should be shown care and respect," he said.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: NRL changes rules to allow Jai Arrow to 'play' 100 games for Souths
World.content:
Jai Arrow will make cameo appearances in the final two rounds of the regular season in order to reach 100 games for South Sydney.

In one of the feel-good stories of the NRL season, the forward who retired with motor neurone disease in May has been approved to start on the field in rounds 26 and 27.

Arrow will then be substituted out in the opening seconds before any active involvement in play.

Arrow, in jersey number 23, has been named co-captain with Cameron Murray, who is listed to come off the bench.

It came after the Rabbitohs made an appeal to the NRL to grant the former Queensland representative an on-field swansong while still able to walk and run.

The initiative gives Arrow two final chances to farewell an NRL career that featured a grand-final appearance in 2021 and 12 State of Origin caps.

The NRL has granted Souths special dispensation to name Arrow as an extra player on today's team list and an extra substitution in their rotation.

Arrow vows to help others fight MND Former NRL player Jai Arrow says he is determined to raise money and awareness for Motor Neurone Disease until a cure is found.

The matches, against Gold Coast and the Sydney Roosters, will bring Arrow's tally to 180 career games and 100 for the Rabbitohs.

Arrow will lead the team out on both occasions and sit on the interchange bench in Souths kit after being substituted out.

The Titans and Roosters have both approved the plan, as have the Rugby League Players Association.

"We are very grateful to Peter [V'landys] and the NRL, and Clint [Newton] at the RLPA, for supporting our proposal," Souths chief executive Blake Solly said.

"We believe this will provide great inspiration for everyone watching the game from the stadium or at home, showing that MND will not hold Jai, or anyone else, back from achieving what they want to achieve in life."

The NRL world has rallied around Arrow since his shock diagnosis and immediate retirement in May.

The league threw Arrow "the world's biggest birthday party" on the day Souths beat Newcastle in July, rolling out a birthday cake in the shape of the 31-year-old's jersey and presenting him with a commemorative jersey.

Fundraising efforts have already passed $1 million in support of Arrow, who is the father of a young daughter.

Players from all clubs have shown their support by marking tries with arrow celebrations throughout the month of July.

World.title: McVeigh to canvass Hird return as icon urges Bombers fans to unite
World.content:
New Essendon coach Mark McVeigh says he will speak to James Hird about returning to the club in a different capacity after a second failed bid to be coach.

McVeigh was unveiled on Tuesday in a press conference that was also attended by a number of Essendon's current players.

Both he and club president Andrew Welsh indicated their desire to have Hird involved.

"I'd love to see James as a part of the club going forward. He's such a fantastic football person," Welsh said.

"I feel there's significant value James can bring, not just tokenistic, but real value to our club and our playing group.

"Certainly, part of my messaging was that Mark and I would want to catch up with him when the time is appropriate."

While Welsh said a pair of calls to Hird had gone unanswered on Monday night, McVeigh said he had shared a conversation with his former captain.

"I love James Hird, he's one of my best mates. It was difficult to go through the process against a good friend," he said.

McVeigh (right) called Hird (left) one of his "best mates" after beating him to the Essendon job. (Getty Images: Ryan Pierse)

"I don't fear those people [Hird's supporters], I actually embrace how they feel, and I understand it, to be fair.

"He's been a constant in my life since I was 17 years of age. We spoke this morning, and the way he spoke of how proud he was of this moment for me, it hasn't broken us, we're still together, but I understand and embrace the feelings of the people that love James Hird, because I do too."

McVeigh, Welsh and club CEO Tim Roberts called for unity at the club amid rumours of a potential board challenge from unimpressed Hird fans.

"I don't ask for your patience, I ask for your re-alignment to our club," McVeigh said.

"I sit here year after year, and we get people coming out of the shadows that want to challenge the board," added Welsh.

"I can tell you since I've been here that this club has never been more united.

"These people want to keep living in the shadows and keep on trying to destabilise our club, we don't jump at shadows.

"We're a strong club and we'll continue to make sure that we make the right decisions on behalf of our members and our teams and our staff to get this club moving forward again."

Tim Watson (pictured) has called for unity at Essendon after Mark McVeigh's signing. (Getty Images: Michael Willson)

The plea for unity came as Essendon legend Tim Watson has the club's passionate supporters to "put [their] weapons down".

"There's got to be a unification of the club now," he told SEN on Tuesday morning.

"People have to put down their weapons and get behind this appointment of a former player — somebody who has been passionate about the football club.

"This is part of the healing process that needs to take place. Ultimately, it's a much bigger thing than the emotion that might be associated with it now. There is an enormous amount of work to do.

Live Moment Look back at Mark McVeigh's first press conference as Essendon's new senior coach. McVeigh says Bombers 'won't live in the past' Pretty good way to end the press conference from the new Essendon coach. He receives another round of applause from those in attendance before walking off the podium. Welsh with another clue on Hird returning I reckon it's going to be a full-court press on the Dons trying to get Hird to say yes to some kind of role within the club. "We have great people that we want to get back involved with the club in meaningful ways," Welsh says. "I look at this as a point that we can re-align that passion." McVeigh with an insight into his game plan McVeigh explains what areas he's going to try and fix on-field. "In the phases of the game, we can't focus on one. If you look at the numbers, we're the bottom of the table in a lot of areas. "I do want them to be brave, I do want them to play with flare, but we do need to fix up our defence. "They [the players] need to come back prepared physically and ready to learn. "The system we'll put in place, you need to understand, otherwise you'll get found out. "When we get all three phases going in the right direction, Essendon will fly." Show more

"Congratulations to him. He's been an Essendon man all his life. He's loved this football club, that was clear in the days that he played.

"He's had a great development profile if you look at where he's been and what he's been doing. He's been part of elite coaching departments [at GWS and Sydney]."

McVeigh has signed a three-year contract with Essendon and was the unanimous choice of the Essendon board.

World.title: Piastri searching for answers as teammate re-enters F1 title picture
World.content:
Oscar Piastri's "disappointing" end to the Dutch Grand Prix has left the Australian and his McLaren team searching for answers, while his teammate has roared back into the Formula 1 title picture.

Last weekend in Zandvoort was shaping to be a good weekend for Piastri.

The Australian was matching the pace at the front through qualifying, and after a terrific second start in the grand prix following Max Verstappen's heavy crash, Piastri was on course for a first podium finish since Miami in May.

Piastri struggles after slow pit stop, Norris wins as Verstappen crashes Reigning world champion Lando Norris has doubled his grand prix win tally in 2026, producing a pair of brilliant overtakes to win the Dutch Grand Prix.

Piastri had performed a breathtaking overtake on Mercedes driver George Russell to move into third and was not far off the pace set by leaders Kimi Antonelli and teammate Lando Norris, despite being on a harder compound tyre.

But a slow first pit stop knocked Piastri back behind Russell and out of third place, and it only got worse from there.

Piastri, who won the Dutch Grand Prix in 2025, fell right off the pace and finished a distant sixth as Norris surged to victory.

Piastri was running third until a slow pit stop knocked him out of the podium position at Zandvoort. (Reuters: Benoit Tessier)

The sudden pace drop-off has left Piastri with plenty of questions that he and the team will want answers to.

"The first stint felt reasonable, but from the second stint onwards, the pace was simply not there, and it became a real struggle," he said.

"We will review the entire weekend and analyse to understand why we experienced such a significant performance drop-off.

"A slow pit stop didn't help, but the fundamental issue was the lack of pace, which is something we'll work on ahead of Monza.

"That's the priority now, to dig into the data with the team to find the root cause and ensure we can move forward in a more positive direction for the upcoming races."

Piastri's situation is a far cry from where he was at the conclusion of last year's Dutch Grand Prix, when he claimed his seventh grand prix win of the season and was the championship leader.

But while Piastri is seeking answers to get back to the front of the grid, Norris is threatening to stay there.

'The fight's still on': Norris re-enters the F1 title picture

McLaren entered the 2026 season having won the previous two constructors' championships, and with Lando Norris as reigning drivers' champion.

Reigning Formula 1 drivers' champion Lando Norris has won the past two grands prix. (Reuters: Benoit Tessier)

But with a new era of regulations, McLaren's 2026 season started poorly.

Piastri crashed on his way to the grid in Melbourne and he and Norris did not start in Shanghai due to car issues.

Norris then had back-to-back retirements in Montreal and Monaco, meaning he failed to finish three of the opening six grands prix.

But the reigning world champion has returned to winning ways, triumphing in Hungary before the mid-year break and then again last weekend in the Netherlands.

With back-to-back wins and growing confidence in his season, Norris has re-emerged as a drivers' championship contender.

F1 drivers' championship standings after Dutch Grand Prix 242 — Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes

183 — George Russell, Mercedes

183 — Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari

159 — Lando Norris, McLaren

155 — Charles Leclerc, Ferrari

With 10 or 11 rounds remaining this season, depending on conflict in the Middle East, Norris is sitting fourth in the standings, 83 points behind leader Kimi Antonelli.

It is a huge gap, but recent history shows it is not an impossible feat.

At the conclusion of last year's Dutch Grand Prix, Max Verstappen was 104 points behind then-leader Piastri with nine rounds remaining.

Verstappen surged towards the end of the season while Piastri slumped. Verstappen fell two points shy of Norris in the standings, but finished a stunning 11 points ahead of Piastri.

Having seen what is possible, Norris has made this year's title fight a four-way race with Antonelli, George Russell and Lewis Hamilton.

Norris's message to his team over the radio after taking the chequered flag on Sunday certainly sounded like the Briton believed his championship hopes are far from over.

"Let's keep pushing. Thank you for the hard work. Let's keep bringing upgrades, let's keep bringing performance, please," he said.

"The fight's still on."

Out of the car, Norris was quick to point out that there is a long season still ahead of the drivers and that he was not getting ahead of himself with an 83-point deficit.

"One race at a time. A lot of people say it now, but it is the truth of it. There's no point in thinking that far ahead," he said after winning on Sunday.

"There are plenty of things we can do better, and we need to do better if we want to fight for a championship.

"We have to keep working hard. There's still plenty of races, plenty of opportunity for everyone."

Norris's deficit to Antonelli was 101 points prior to the weekend in Hungary, but the McLaren champion has reduced that by 18 with two tremendous weekends.

However, the 83-point gap is significant and Antonelli has extended his overall championship lead.

Entering the Dutch Grand Prix weekend, the young Italian's lead over Hamilton was 50 points, and 59 over Russell.

After the weekend, his lead is 59 points over both Hamilton and Russell.

F1 heads to Monza for the Italian Grand Prix in two weeks, one of the fastest tracks on the calendar and vastly different to the tight and twisting circuits in Hungary and the Netherlands where Norris has won this year.

World.title: 'A dangerous individual': Ex-snooker champ convicted of child sex abuse
World.content:
Former world snooker champion Graeme Dott has been convicted of sexually abusing two primary school children in Scotland in the 1990s and early 2000s.

Dott, 49, was found guilty of abusing a girl from 1993-96 and a boy from 2006-10 after a five-day trial at the High Court in Glasgow. The judge ordered Dott to be held in custody ahead of his sentencing on September 29.

The woman, now in her 40s, testified that Dott sexually abused her on multiple occasions, "caressing" her bottom over her clothing, exposing himself and touching her with parts of his body, including his penis.

The man, now in his late 20s, said he was abused on multiple occasions, with Dott touching him inappropriately, kissing him and performing sexual acts.

Dott with his wife Elaine after winning the snooker world championship in 2006. (Getty Images: Rui Vieira)

"Dott is a dangerous individual, and I hope this conviction provides some measure of comfort to those impacted by his crimes," Detective Inspector Gary Smillie from Police Scotland said.

Snooker's governing body suspended Dott in April 2025 after he was charged in the case. The Scot was ranked number 56 in the world at the time and dropped from the rankings after the season.

On Monday, the World Professional Billiards and Snooker Association revoked Dott's membership following an emergency board meeting. The WPBSA also said it wrote to the World Snooker Tour to request his immediate removal from the WST Hall of Fame.

Dott won the World Snooker Championship in 2006 and was a runner-up twice.

AP/Reuters

World.title: Zak Butters trade rumours dominate Port Adelaide's turbulent season
World.content:
It's been a tumultuous year for Port Adelaide.

Its newly-appointed coach Josh Carr had to navigate a new system with an injury riddled list; using 39 of its 44-listed players and finishing the season with 15 unavailable.

He also had to build chemistry and belief despite a contract decision overshadowing his campaign.

Its vice-captain and dual All-Australian Zak Butters has dominated headlines all season as one of the biggest free-agents available this off-season; and has now confirmed the worst-kept secret in football that he has requested a trade to Victoria.

"I've made a decision to head home. It's obviously been one that I've wrestled with for a while now. It's been a tough decision and one that I haven't taken lightly," Butters said on Monday.

"Although I've loved my time in Adelaide … I'm probably at a stage in my life where I'd like to get back around some family and friends and enjoy some more time with them."

Butters denied reports in June that he had begun telling those close to him he was eager to move east after a trip back home during the round 12 bye; another chapter in a compendium of updates on the dual Showdown medallist's future.

So why was the club so protective of Butters when he had a foot out the door?

There are two key foundations of any negotiation in any industry. Value and relationships.

Growing speculation

As the weeks progressed and the speculation grew, the four-horse race between Richmond, Geelong, Collingwood and the Western Bulldogs intensified as the coverage evolved into a public bidding war; increasing Butters' contract terms and giving the Power fuel for higher trade demands.

Every story has a source … and every source has an agenda.

Zak Butters to leave Port Adelaide Star Port Adelaide midfielder Zak Butters has informed the Power he wants to return to Victoria.

Player agents are looking to maximise demand and clubs want their outgoing stars to leave at a high price.

Relationships between the two parties are also incredibly important in future dealings. Clubs are constantly trying to find the balance between fair compensation and long-term favours.

For Port Adelaide this was the case two years ago when Dan Houston was desperate to move to Collingwood but the Magpies didn't have the capital for a reasonable return.

The Power settled for Picks 13, 29 and 36 plus forwards Jack Lukosius and Joe Richards in exchange for its dual All-Australian defender and a future first round pick.

It was a move that was widely panned at the time but hasn't done much damage given rising key forward Jack Whitlock was taken at 29 and Joe Richards is developing into a handy midfield option.

But Dan Houston and Zak Butters are different cases.

The Power is hoping to maximise its draft haul in moving its triple best-and-fairest winner given it has rarely had early selections in recent years leading to a gulf in young talent depth.

It also has a litany of upcoming academy and father-son draftees it will need to match bids on, such as expected number one pick Dougie Cochrane and Zemes Pilot.

Matthew Richardson spoke about the Butters trade rumous in May. (ABC News: Marco Catalano)

Back in May, Port chief executive Matthew Richardson flagged on ABC Sport that the club would match any bid on Butters to force a trade given the star is a restricted free agent.

"There will be offers that we can match and we will match. It does give the club a fair bit of control in what happens," he said.

The issue is Butters current suitors have a diverse availability of picks at their disposal and the Power's best option Richmond doesn't quite align with the values Butters claimed he was eyeing when I asked him back in March what would dictate his decision.

"I think you're stupid if you don't want to win premierships," he said.

"I want to win. Family is important as well … but you can't look too far ahead."

THE CONTENDERS (As of current ladder position, all four clubs have all future picks available) Geelong: 17, 35, 53, 71

Western Bulldogs: 10, 28, 46

Collingwood: 16, 34, 63, 66, 70

Richmond: 2, 20, 38, 56

While Port navigates its way through the 20 out-of-contract players it has held fire on due to the Butters decision, there will be time for Josh Carr to reflect on his inaugural season at the helm.

Season highlights

Despite double ups with four sides who missed finals; the Power managed seven wins in 2026 and had a clear narrative throughout; it could match it with the best but could rarely beat them.

Its campaign ended with an equal league record five losses by five-points or less and eight by as much as 14-points.

A Showdown win over Adelaide in June was the highlight, plus its April upset over Geelong; but its only road wins were against fellow bottom four sides West Coast and Richmond.

It finished 16th for ball movement from D50 to F50 but defensively was a powerhouse until the final month where 10-goal losses to the Lions, Swans and Demons blew out the team's average points against to 89, dropping it down from a Top 4 side into 10th.

The other positive was its clearance work. Despite missing Connor Rozee for the majority of the campaign, and Zak Butters for the final month, the side finished second for clearance differential, blooding future stars in Jase Burgoyne, Joe Richards and Miles Bergman on ball.

Port Adelaide won seven games in the 2026 season. (ABC Riverland: Catherine Heuzenroeder)

From a list perspective it was the only side not to have a player named in the AFL's 22-under-22 squad and some of the long-term signings from the Hinkley era like Todd Marshall and Brandon Zerk-Thatcher barely featured.

Former Port midfielder and four times Showdown medallist Josh Francou believes 2026 was a free hit for Josh Carr.

"It has been a difficult campaign … the way they're defending the ground is a real plus for them but they struggle to move the ball," he said.

"Next year things start to ramp up on Josh Carr and he's got to get it right."

Despite all the adversities, it feels like Josh Carr has laid the foundation for success but a critical off-season awaits as he looks to reshape the list and keep his stars healthy for the 2027 campaign.

World.title: Cyclists run for cover as hailstorm forces La Vuelta stage cancellation
World.content:
A torrential hailstorm in the French Pyrenees forced the abandonment of the third stage of the Vuelta a España on Monday.

With 15 kilometres remaining of the 174-km route from Gruissan to Font-Romeu, the skies darkened as the peloton neared the top of the Col de Mont-Louis and huge hailstones began bouncing off the tarmac and pelting the riders.

Mats Wenzel (Kern Pharma) and Lorenzo Fortunato (XDS Astana) were 25 seconds ahead of the peloton when the elements intervened, as race leader and favourite Tadej Pogacar was seen indicating to the peloton to pull off the course.

Bedraggled riders were then seen getting off their bikes and shuffling into a hotel for shelter.

Shortly afterwards, race organisers, ASO, announced the stage would not resume, leaving fans frustrated at the finish where thick layers of hail blanketed the road.

Slovenia's Pogacar (UAE Emirates-XRG) retained his overall lead of nine seconds from Belgium's Wout van Aert (Dutch Visma-Lease a Bike) with Britain's Matt Brennan 10 seconds back.

Earlier it had been warm and sunny on the flat approaches to the mountainous finish with no sign of the chaos to come as a five-man breakaway group stayed out ahead.

Pogacar, bidding to complete his Grand Tour collection by winning the Vuelta for the first time, was always near the front of the pack with his team setting the pace.

Sadly, his expected challenge for the stage victory fell foul of the weather in an anticlimactic finish.

He will get his chance to underline his superiority again on Tuesday, though with stage four featuring three first-category climbs as the race starts and finishes in Andorra la Vella.

Reuters

Tech.title: Polestar claims it was blindsided by sales ban
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Polestar said the Trump administration strung it along for months before finally rejecting its request to continue selling its electric vehicles in the US under a rule outlawing vehicles with connected software from China.

In an August 18th letter sent to dealers and obtained by The Verge, Polestar said it doesn’t have a clear answer as to why its application to continue selling its EVs in the US was denied, considering its sister company Volvo was authorized to sell its vehicles despite similar corporate ownership. (The letter was first reported by The Wall Street Journal.)

The US Department of Commerce approved Volvo in May 2026 to continue importing and selling its vehicles in the US, despite restrictions tied to its majority Chinese owner, Geely. But one month later, the department rejected Polestar’s similar request, leading to the company to announce it would stop selling its vehicles in the US starting with the 2027 model year. The rule, which originated under the Biden administration, bans the import and sale of vehicles with connected software from hostile countries, including China.

In the letter to dealers, Polestar’s head of product Peter Wexler lays out the timeline of the company’s communications with the Trump administration, starting with a May 29, 2025 application to the

Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) under the Commerce Department. In subsequent meetings, Wexler says Polestar was given the impression that Polestar would be approved, considering its vehicles are functionally similar to Volvo’s.

Jeffrey Kessler, Under Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Security, said during an in-person meeting with Polestar’s representatives “that it would be reasonable for Polestar to expect approval of its applications if Volvo Cars was approved to sell its cars under effectively the same shareholding and ownership structure and with the same hardware and software in the Polestar 3 as the Volvo EX90,” Wexler writes.

Polestar told the administration it open to a variety of “mitigation measures” to ensure its vehicles were compliant with the ban on Chinese software, including regular audits, geographic restrictions on data storage and management, and limitations on digital keys and remote access. But the administration declined all such offers, Wexler said.

“BIS never engaged in any such discussions with Polestar,” he writes. “Instead, BIS communicated that it had all the information it required to render a decision.”

Wexler said that Polestar is continuing to press the administration for an explanation on why it was denied approval. The company was sued recently by Polestar dealer Prestige Imports in New Jersey, which accuses the company of engineering its own exit from the US by failing to do enough to satisfy regulators at the Commerce Department.

Tech.title: Apple’s ‘new’ polishing cloth is the same except $10 cheaper
Tech.content:

Apple just dropped a new polishing cloth, and unlike its refreshed Mac Mini models, it comes with a price cut, as spotted earlier by MacRumors. The polishing cloth is still “made with soft, nonabrasive material” but costs $9 instead of $19.

It doesn’t look like anything else has changed, as the description matches an archived version of Apple’s old polishing cloth, which it no longer lists on its website.
